meta.blurb: Sir Charles Baskerville is found dead on a lonely path, and beside him are the prints of a giant dog. Now his heir comes home to the house on the moor. Watson goes with him, and something howls in the dark.
meta.bible: Sherlock Holmes: the great London detective, calm, sharp, and fond of surprises. Dr Watson: his friend and the narrator's point of view, loyal and honest. Dr Mortimer: a kind country doctor and friend of Sir Charles. Sir Henry Baskerville: the young heir, newly arrived from Canada. Sir Charles Baskerville: Sir Henry's uncle, who died on the yew path at Baskerville Hall; weak heart. Hugo Baskerville: a cruel ancestor in the old manuscript. Barrymore: the butler at Baskerville Hall. Mrs Barrymore: his wife; her younger brother is the convict Selden. Jack Stapleton: a naturalist who collects butterflies near Merripit House; really a Baskerville and the villain. Beryl Stapleton: Jack's wife, who pretends to be his sister. Laura Lyons: a woman of Coombe Tracey who wrote to Sir Charles. Mr Frankland: a quarrelsome old neighbour with a telescope. Selden: the escaped convict, killed in Sir Henry's old clothes. Inspector Lestrade: the Scotland Yard detective. Baskerville Hall: the old family house. Grimpen Mire: the dangerous bog on the moor. Dartmoor: the wild moor. Devonshire: the county. Merripit House: the Stapletons' house. Coombe Tracey: the village where Laura Lyons lives. Baker Street: where Holmes lives. London. Canada. Scotland Yard. Rodger Baskerville: Sir Charles's younger brother, who left England in disgrace and was said to have died in Central America; Stapleton's father. Beryl Garcia: Beryl's maiden name; a beauty of Costa Rica. Cartwright: Holmes's quick young messenger, who brings supplies to the hut. John Clayton: the cabman who drove the bearded man in London. Mrs Hudson: Holmes's landlady at Baker Street. Selden: the escaped convict from Princetown prison. Princetown: the prison on the moor. Lafter Hall: Mr Frankland's house, with a telescope on its roof. Yew Alley: the dark path of yew trees at Baskerville Hall, with a gate to the moor. Northumberland Hotel: where Sir Henry stays in London. Charing Cross, Bond Street, Regent Street, Paddington: places in London. Grimpen: the village where Dr Mortimer lives. Central America, Costa Rica, Yorkshire: places in Stapleton's past. The Civil War: the time of Hugo Baskerville. Mire: the Great Grimpen Mire, with a secret path marked by white sticks and an island with an old tin mine. Fixed facts: the manuscript is dated 1742 and was written for two sons. Hugo's victim was a farmer's daughter who died of fear and tiredness on the moor. Stapleton's school in the north failed after a pupil died of fever. The warning letter was cut from a newspaper by Beryl and smelled of white jessamine. The old black boot was stolen from Sir Henry's hotel to give the hound a scent. Selden died in Sir Henry's old clothes, which Barrymore gave him. Stapleton was lost in the Mire; his body was never found. Holmes lived secretly in a stone hut on the tor, and Watson did not know until he found him there. Beat 200: Holmes and Watson go to the opera in London. Voice and tone: tense, clear and clever, a mystery told step by step; deaths are stated plainly, with no gore; the hound is a real dog covered in glowing phosphorus, not a ghost.

beats.scene: A walking stick leans against the door of a Baker Street sitting room

beats.scene: A boy searches a waste-paper basket in a hotel lobby

beats.scene: Holmes writes a telegram at a desk as Watson watches over his shoulder

beats.scene: A spaniel sits at Dr Mortimer's feet as red fields slide past the window

beats.scene: Two soldiers with rifles stand guard on a small country platform

beats.scene: A horse and carriage rattles down a green lane between high banks

beats.scene: A lone soldier on horseback sits black against the grey moor sky

beats.scene: Barrymore stands tall in the doorway, black-bearded and pale, with a lantern
beats.summary: Barrymore the butler and his wife welcome Sir Henry to the Hall.

beats.summary: Stapleton, a naturalist from Merripit House, greets Watson and knows who he is.

beats.scene: Old stone huts sit in circles on a rocky hillside at sunset
beats.summary: Watson sees the ruined stone huts of ancient men on his way back.

beats.scene: Watson tells Sir Henry about the day beside the fire in the great hall

beats.summary: Watson's first report tells Holmes about the moor, the soldiers and the escaped convict.

beats.summary: Watson lists the neighbours: the Stapletons, Mortimer and Mr Frankland.

beats.scene: Sir Henry smiles at Beryl as they stand together on the open moor
beats.summary: On a walk, Sir Henry meets Beryl Stapleton again, and she is kinder.

beats.scene: Stapleton strides over the grass, pale with anger, to seize his sister's arm

beats.scene: Sir Henry frowns on the path with his fists on his hips
beats.summary: Sir Henry is offended and puzzled by Stapleton's anger.

beats.scene: Stapleton bows humbly to Sir Henry, holding his hat in the hall
beats.summary: Stapleton calls at the Hall to apologise and invites them to dinner.

beats.scene: A low grey house stands among twisted trees on a darkening moor
beats.summary: Sir Henry and Watson walk to Merripit House at dusk.

beats.scene: Stapleton shows rows of pinned butterflies in glass cases to his guests
beats.summary: Stapleton shows his butterfly collection and speaks of his old school.

beats.scene: A pale woman sits silently at a candlelit table, looking at her plate
beats.summary: At dinner Beryl is silent, and Watson sees fear in her eyes.

beats.scene: Two men walk quickly across a starlit moor, glancing over their shoulders
beats.summary: On the walk home a long howl echoes over the moor.

beats.scene: Watson lies awake in bed as a thin light creeps under his door
beats.summary: Watson wakes at night and sees Barrymore creeping past with a candle.

beats.scene: Barrymore holds a candle against a high window that faces the moor
beats.summary: He watches Barrymore stand at a window, holding the candle up to the dark.

beats.scene: Sir Henry and Watson talk quietly over breakfast in the great hall
beats.summary: Next day Watson tells Sir Henry, and they plan to catch Barrymore.

beats.scene: Two men sit watching a dark corridor through a half-open door
beats.summary: The next night they wait in the dark, and the hours drag on.

beats.scene: Sir Henry bursts into a bare room where Barrymore stands at the window
beats.summary: They follow Barrymore and find him signalling from the window.

beats.scene: Barrymore trembles, with the candle shaking in his hand
beats.summary: Barrymore confesses that the candle is a signal to a man on the moor.

beats.scene: A tiny light twinkles in the black distance beyond the window

beats.scene: A tall thin man stands black on a high rock against the moon
beats.summary: The convict escapes, but Watson sees a stranger standing on a hill.

beats.scene: Sir Henry hands a bundle of old clothes to Barrymore in a morning room
beats.summary: Barrymore thanks them, and Sir Henry gives him old clothes for the convict.

beats.scene: Barrymore speaks in a low voice beside the tall window of the hall
beats.summary: Barrymore reports that Selden has seen another man hiding on the moor.

beats.scene: Barrymore holds out a scrap of burned paper in his open palm
beats.summary: Barrymore shows a burned scrap of letter that he found after Sir Charles died.

beats.scene: Dr Mortimer reads the burned scrap by the window of the great hall

beats.scene: A red-faced white-haired old man waves a stick at a gate
beats.summary: On the road Watson meets Mr Frankland, who loves lawsuits.

beats.scene: An old man points a large brass telescope from a flat roof
beats.summary: Frankland proudly shows Watson the telescope he uses to watch the moor.

beats.scene: A graceful woman sits at a table with a typewriter in a small room
beats.summary: In Coombe Tracey Watson finds Laura Lyons, a beautiful woman with a typewriter.

beats.scene: Laura Lyons twists a handkerchief as Watson sits across from her
beats.summary: Laura admits that she wrote to Sir Charles to ask for money.

beats.scene: Laura Lyons shakes her head firmly as Watson waits for an answer
beats.summary: She says she asked Sir Charles to meet her at the gate but never went.

beats.scene: Watson stands on a quiet lane, looking back at a small house
beats.summary: Watson feels sure that she is hiding a name, and he leaves.

beats.scene: Frankland points his telescope at a boy climbing a distant hill
beats.summary: Frankland says that a boy carries food every day to a hidden man on a tor.

beats.scene: Sir Henry and Watson talk at the Hall door as the afternoon sun fades
beats.summary: Sir Henry is invited to dine at Merripit, so Watson plans a quick trip to the tor.

beats.scene: Watson climbs a steep rocky slope under a hot, empty sky
beats.summary: Watson climbs the rocky hill toward the old stone huts.

beats.scene: Watson looks into a small stone hut with a blanket and tins
beats.summary: In one hut Watson finds a camp, with a blanket, tins and a water bottle.

beats.scene: A hand holds a half-sheet of paper beside a blanket on the floor
beats.summary: He finds a note that reports Dr Watson's own movements.

beats.scene: Watson crouches with his revolver as a shadow crosses the hut door
beats.summary: Someone is coming, and Watson waits with his revolver.

beats.scene: Sherlock Holmes stands smiling in the moonlit doorway of the stone hut
beats.summary: The hidden man is Sherlock Holmes himself.

beats.scene: Holmes and Watson sit talking quietly inside the stone hut
beats.summary: Holmes explains that he came secretly to watch the moor.

beats.scene: Holmes points at a high rock where a lonely figure once stood
beats.summary: Holmes was the man on the tor, and Cartwright is the boy with food.

beats.scene: Holmes springs up in alarm and snatches his hat
beats.summary: Holmes learns that Sir Henry dines at Merripit and rushes to protect him.

beats.scene: Holmes and Watson hurry down a rocky slope as the sun sets
beats.summary: Holmes and Watson run down from the tor as evening falls.

beats.scene: Two men walk fast along a dim moor path with revolvers ready
beats.summary: Holmes says he fears for Sir Henry and checks his revolver.

beats.scene: A terrible scream breaks the silence of the dark, still moor
beats.summary: A terrible human scream rings out across the moor.

beats.scene: Holmes and Watson run over dark rocks toward a fading cry
beats.summary: They run toward the cry, and a distant howl follows it.

beats.scene: A dark body lies face down at the foot of a rocky slope
beats.summary: They find a body lying at the foot of the rocks.

beats.scene: Holmes strikes a match above a pale bearded face
beats.summary: Holmes lights a match and shows that the dead man is Selden.

beats.scene: Holmes studies a tweed jacket on the dead man in the match light
beats.summary: The dead man wears Sir Henry's old clothes, which explains everything.

beats.scene: Holmes and Watson search the dark slope as a distant howl fades
beats.summary: They search for the hound, but find only silence.

beats.scene: A thin man with a butterfly net walks quickly toward the two detectives
beats.summary: Stapleton arrives and asks if Sir Henry has been hurt.

beats.scene: Stapleton stands pale and silent beside the body of the convict
beats.summary: Stapleton is shocked to see Holmes, and seems more disappointed than sad.

beats.scene: Stapleton nods gravely beside the body, holding his net and green box
beats.summary: Stapleton asks how Selden died and agrees to send word to the police.

beats.scene: Holmes whispers to Watson as a lamp moves away over the moor
beats.summary: Holmes notes that Stapleton seemed to expect Sir Henry to be the victim.

beats.scene: Sir Henry rises from an armchair in surprise as Holmes walks into the hall
beats.summary: At dawn Holmes appears at the Hall, and Sir Henry is astonished.

beats.scene: Barrymore bows his head beside his weeping wife in the kitchen
beats.summary: Barrymore and his wife learn that Selden is dead.

beats.scene: Holmes holds a lamp before an old portrait in a long dark gallery
beats.summary: Holmes studies the portraits in the gallery until he reaches Hugo Baskerville.

beats.scene: Holmes hides the cavalier's hat and curls with his hand, staring at the face
beats.summary: Covering Hugo's hat and curls, Holmes sees that the face is Stapleton's.

beats.scene: Holmes explains the likeness to Watson with a long finger pointed at the painting

beats.summary: Holmes tells her that Stapleton is married, and she is stunned.

beats.summary: Holmes explains his plan to Sir Henry and Lestrade at the Hall.

beats.summary: At dusk Holmes, Watson and Lestrade walk out to find a hiding place.

beats.summary: Holmes notices a white fog rising from the Grimpen Mire.

beats.scene: Holmes lies flat with his ear to the cold ground
beats.summary: The fog thickens, and Holmes moves them close to the path.

beats.summary: They wait in the cold, listening, as the night grows later.

beats.summary: The fog rolls in like a wall, and Holmes hears something coming.

beats.summary: Sir Henry walks right past the hidden watchers, unaware of the danger.

beats.summary: A huge black hound with a burning mouth springs out of the fog.

A1A2: A walking stick sat by the door in Holmes and Watson's room.
Watson read the name James Mortimer on a silver band on the stick.
Watson said the stick belonged to an old doctor who lived in the country.
Holmes said no, the owner was a young man who had left a London hospital.
Holmes showed Watson the marks of a dog's teeth on the handle.
Watson looked in a big book and found a Dr Mortimer in Grimpen.
Soon a tall, thin man came in with a small brown dog.
Dr Mortimer touched Holmes's head and said that it was a very fine shape.
Dr Mortimer sat down and said that he was afraid and needed help.
Dr Mortimer took out an old yellow paper and began to read it aloud.
The old paper was written long ago by a man called Baskerville.
Hugo Baskerville was a wild, cruel man who lived at Baskerville Hall.
Hugo liked a farmer's daughter, but she was afraid and kept away from him.
One night Hugo and his friends took the girl from her father's farm.
They locked the girl in a room and sat downstairs drinking and singing.
The girl was very afraid, so she climbed out of the window and ran.
Hugo found the room empty and shouted that he would give his soul to catch her.
His friends rode after him, and a shepherd told them he had seen something terrible.
They found the girl dead, and Hugo lay dead beside a huge black dog.
The paper said, keep away from the moor in the dark hours of the night.
Holmes called the story a fairy tale, but Mortimer had more to say.
Sir Charles Baskerville was a kind man who had a lot of money.
Sir Charles had a weak heart, and he was afraid of the old curse.
Every evening after dinner he walked down the Yew Alley with a cigar.
One night he did not come home, so Barrymore went out to look.
Barrymore found the gate to the moor open at the end of the path.
Dr Mortimer saw no wound on the body, but the face looked terrible.
Mortimer saw some very big footprints in the soft ground near the body.
Mortimer said, in a low voice, that they were the prints of a giant hound.
Sir Henry was coming from Canada, and Mortimer asked Holmes for help.
Holmes told Mortimer to meet Sir Henry, and then he thought all night.
The next morning Sir Henry came, a strong young man with dark eyes.
Sir Henry showed Holmes a strange letter that came to his hotel.
The letter said, keep away from the moor, in words cut from a newspaper.
Holmes said the words came from yesterday's newspaper, cut with small scissors.
Holmes held the paper to his nose, but he did not say why.
Sir Henry had lost a brand new brown boot from outside his hotel room.
Sir Henry said he was not afraid, and he was going to his home.
Holmes told them to come back for lunch, and then he followed them.
In the street a man with a black beard watched Sir Henry from a cab.
Holmes went to look at paintings all morning and said nothing about the case.
At the hotel Sir Henry was angry because an old black boot was gone.
Later they found his new brown boot again, but not the old one.
Holmes sent for Cartwright, a clever boy who ran errands in London.
Cartwright went to many hotels to look for a newspaper with holes.
Holmes sent a message to the Hall to ask if Barrymore was there.
A cab driver named John Clayton came to see Holmes at Baker Street.
Clayton said that his passenger had told him he was Sherlock Holmes.
Holmes wrote down all the facts and said that the moor must be watched.
Holmes could not leave London, so he asked Watson to go with Sir Henry.
At the station Holmes told Watson to keep Sir Henry safe day and night.
The three men rode west in the train, and Sir Henry looked out.
At the small station on the moor, they saw two soldiers with guns.
A soldier told them that a bad prisoner had escaped from the prison.
The carriage drove along narrow lanes with high green banks on each side.
Then the moor opened out, wide and grey, and a soldier sat on a horse.
They came to the gates of Baskerville Hall and drove up a long avenue.
Barrymore, the tall butler, stood at the door with his pale wife.
At dinner, the dark old room and the portraits made Sir Henry uneasy.
In the night Watson heard a woman crying, and next morning her eyes were red.
Watson went for a long walk across the wide moor alone.
A thin man with a butterfly net ran up and said hello.
The man, Stapleton, said he caught butterflies and once had a school.
Stapleton showed Watson a green place called the Mire, which was very dangerous.
A low, sad sound rolled across the moor, and Stapleton said it was a bird.
Stapleton saw a rare butterfly and ran across the soft ground after it.
A dark woman ran to Watson and said, go back to London.
Then she saw her mistake, because Watson was not Sir Henry.
On the way home Watson saw old stone huts on the hill.
That evening Watson told Sir Henry about his day and began a letter.
Watson wrote a long letter to Holmes about the moor and the convict.
He also wrote a list of the people who lived near the Hall.
A week later Sir Henry met Beryl on the moor, and she was kind.
Suddenly Stapleton ran up, very angry, and pulled his sister away.
Sir Henry felt hurt and did not understand why Stapleton was so angry.
The next day Stapleton came to say sorry and asked them to dinner.
On Friday Sir Henry and Watson walked to Merripit House as night came.
Stapleton showed them his butterflies and told them about his old school.
At dinner Beryl said very little, and Watson saw that she was afraid.
On the way home they heard a long, sad cry on the moor.
One night Watson woke up and saw Barrymore walking by with a candle.
Barrymore stood at a window and held the candle up to the dark.
In the morning Watson told Sir Henry, and they made a plan.
The next night they sat in the dark and waited for hours.
At last they followed Barrymore and found him at the window again.
Barrymore shook and said the candle was a signal to a man outside.
The man was Selden, the brother of Mrs Barrymore, who loved him.
A small light answered from far away, so Sir Henry decided to go.
Sir Henry and Watson ran across the moor after the wild man.
The man escaped, but then Watson saw a tall stranger on a rock.
Barrymore thanked them, and Sir Henry gave him some old clothes for Selden.
Barrymore said Selden had seen another man hiding on the moor.
Barrymore showed Watson a burned piece of paper from Sir Charles's fire.
Dr Mortimer said the letters L L were for Laura Lyons of Coombe Tracey.
On the road Watson met Mr Frankland, an old man who loved lawsuits.
Mr Frankland showed Watson a big telescope on his roof.
In Coombe Tracey, Watson met Laura Lyons, a pretty woman with a typewriter.
Laura said that she had written to Sir Charles and asked for money.
She asked him to meet her at the gate, but she never went.
Watson was sure that she was hiding a name, and he went home.
Frankland said a boy carried food to a man on a hill every day.
Sir Henry was to eat at Merripit, so Watson went to the hill quickly.
Watson climbed the rocky hill toward the old stone huts.
In one hut he found a blanket, some tins and a bottle of water.
On the floor he also found a paper about Watson's own journeys.
Watson held his gun and waited, because someone was coming nearer.
A man stepped into the door, and it was Sherlock Holmes.
Holmes said he had come in secret to watch the moor and its people.
Holmes was the man on the rock, and Cartwright was the boy.
Then Holmes heard that Sir Henry was at Merripit and jumped up in fear.
Holmes and Watson ran down the hill as the sun went down.
Holmes said that he feared for Sir Henry, and he checked his gun.
Suddenly a terrible scream rang out across the dark moor.
They ran toward the scream, and then a deep, sad sound came from far away.
At the foot of some rocks they found a body on the ground.
Holmes lit a match, and Watson saw that the dead man was Selden.
Selden was wearing Sir Henry's old clothes, and Holmes understood why.
They looked everywhere for the hound, but they found nothing at all.
Stapleton came out of the dark and asked if Sir Henry was hurt.
Stapleton was shocked to see Holmes and looked almost disappointed at the body.
Stapleton asked how the man died and said he would call the police.
Holmes told Watson that Stapleton had looked for Sir Henry, not Selden.
At dawn Holmes walked into the Hall, and Sir Henry was amazed.
Barrymore and his wife learned that their dear Selden was dead.
Holmes took a lamp into the gallery and looked at the old portraits.
He covered Hugo's hat and hair, and saw Stapleton's face.
Holmes explained that Stapleton must be a Baskerville by blood.
Holmes and Watson went to see Laura Lyons in Coombe Tracey.
Holmes told her that Stapleton was married, and she was shocked.
Laura told the truth, and later Lestrade came from London by train.
Holmes told Sir Henry and Lestrade his plan at the Hall.
Sir Henry said that he was not afraid and would go to dinner.
Holmes told Sir Henry to keep to the path and never run away.
At dusk the three men walked out onto the moor with their guns.
They hid behind some rocks near the lights of Merripit House.
Soon Holmes saw a white fog rising from the Mire.
The fog grew thicker, so Holmes moved them nearer to the path.
They waited a long time in the cold, listening to the night.
At last Sir Henry came out of Merripit House and began to walk.
The fog covered the path, and Holmes heard something coming through it.
Sir Henry walked right past the three men, and he did not see them.
Then a huge black hound jumped out of the fog with a glowing mouth.
The three men fired their guns as the hound ran after Sir Henry.
Sir Henry screamed and ran, but the hound caught him and threw him down.
Holmes ran forward and fired again and again into the great dog.
The hound lay dead, and Sir Henry was safe but very weak.
Holmes touched the dog's mouth, and his fingers glowed in the dark.
Sir Henry sat up, and Holmes said it was only a living dog.
Lestrade stayed with the dog while Holmes and Watson searched the house.
In an upstairs room they found Beryl tied up, and they set her free.
Beryl told Holmes that she was Stapleton's wife, and not his sister.
She said that Stapleton had run into the Mire to a hidden island.
The men carried Sir Henry to the house, and the fog hid everything.
In the morning the fog cleared, and Beryl showed them the path.
They followed a line of white sticks across the soft ground.
On the island they found a stake, a chain and a heap of bones.
Holmes picked up an old black boot from the muddy path.
The boot was Sir Henry's, and it had given the hound his scent.
Stapleton's footprints stopped at the edge of the deep green mud.
Holmes said that the Mire never gives back what it takes.
Days later, Holmes sat by the fire and began to explain everything.
Stapleton was the son of Rodger Baskerville, the brother of Sir Charles.
Rodger left England in disgrace and was thought to have died alone.
His son became a teacher in the north, but his school failed.
Stapleton had married Beryl, a lovely girl from Costa Rica, and they moved to Devon.
Stapleton learned that only two men stood between him and the estate.
Dr Mortimer had told Stapleton about the old story and Sir Charles's heart.
Stapleton bought a huge, fierce dog and took it secretly to the moor.
He covered the dog with a paste that shone brightly in the dark.
Laura Lyons wrote a letter that brought Sir Charles to the moor gate.
Sir Charles waited at the gate, and then he saw the hound coming.
Sir Charles ran down the alley in fear until his heart stopped.
Stapleton led the hound away, and he thought no law could stop him.
Stapleton followed Sir Henry to London and wore a false black beard.
Beryl had secretly written the warning letter, and it smelled of white flowers.
Stapleton paid someone to take Sir Henry's boot for the hound.
Beryl would not help him trap Sir Henry, and Stapleton became very angry.
Selden wore Sir Henry's old clothes, and the hound followed that smell.
Holmes said that he had risked Sir Henry's life, but he needed proof.
Holmes finished his story, and the old clock struck midnight in the hall.
Dr Mortimer said Sir Henry needed rest and a long journey by sea.
Selden was buried quietly, and Barrymore and his wife stood by the grave.
Barrymore told Sir Henry that he and his wife would go away.
Mr Frankland came to the Hall and boasted about his famous telescope.
Holmes told Lestrade that Laura Lyons was a victim, not a criminal.
Beryl left the moor with a small bag to live somewhere quiet.
Sir Henry opened the windows of the great hall and let the sun in.
On their last night, Holmes and Watson stood at the moor gate.
At a farewell dinner, Sir Henry thanked Holmes and Watson warmly.
The next morning the trunks were packed, and everyone got ready to go.
Sir Henry thanked Holmes and said he would come back some day.
The carriage passed Merripit House, which was now silent and empty.
From the carriage Watson saw the moor, calm and bright in the sun.
Sir Henry and Dr Mortimer left on a train, with the little dog.
Lestrade said goodbye and said he would never forget the hound.
Holmes and Watson rode the train back to London and talked.
Holmes said that it had been one of his strangest cases.
They arrived in London at night, and a cab took them home.
Mrs Hudson welcomed them, and Holmes sat warming his feet by the fire.
That evening in Baker Street, Holmes asked Watson to go to the opera.
B1B2: A visitor had called at Baker Street the night before and left a heavy walking stick behind. Dr Watson had been out, but at breakfast he found Holmes looking at it with great interest.

A silver band on the stick carries the name of Dr James Mortimer and a few kind words from his friends. Holmes, who is busy with his breakfast and does not turn round, asks Watson what he thinks of the owner.
Watson looks at the worn handle and decides that the owner must be an old, popular country doctor. Such a man, he says, would be thanked by his patients with a gift like this one.
Holmes smiles and says that the guess is good but not quite right. The gift came from friends at a London hospital, he explains, and the doctor was probably young when he left to work in the country.

Holmes then points out the deep marks of teeth on the handle, made by a dog that often carries the stick for its master. The marks are too wide for a terrier and too small for a mastiff, so the dog is likely a spaniel.

Watson, who still cannot believe it, takes down a thick book listing every doctor in the land. He finds a Dr James Mortimer who lives in Grimpen, a village on the edge of Dartmoor, and Holmes looks very pleased.

A cab stops outside, and a moment later a tall, thin man hurries in with a brown spaniel at his heel. He has a long nose, kind grey eyes and a stoop, and he says at once that he has come back for his stick.

Dr Mortimer cannot help staring at Holmes's head, and he asks if he may touch it. He says, with a nervous laugh, that he would love to see such a fine skull in a museum, and Holmes thanks him politely.
Holmes asks him to sit down and to tell them what is wrong. Mortimer, twisting his hands, says that he is a man of science, but he faces a puzzle that no science can explain.

Holmes sits back in his chair, closes his eyes and joins his fingertips, as he always does when he is ready to listen. Dr Mortimer unfolds a yellow paper, clears his throat and starts to read in a high, cracking voice.

Dr Mortimer explains that the manuscript was written in the year 1742 by a Baskerville for his two sons. The writer had the story from his own father, and he wants his sons to know why they must be careful.

In the days of the Civil War, he says, Baskerville Hall belonged to a man named Hugo, who was wild, godless and cruel. Nobody in the neighbourhood loved him, and the servants feared the sound of his boots on the stairs.

One autumn, Hugo fell in love with the daughter of a farmer who lived near his lands. The girl, who had heard stories of his evil name, kept out of his way and would not even look at him when he passed.

On a dark night Hugo and five or six of his drinking friends crept to the farm while the girl's father and brothers were away. They carried her off and brought her to the Hall, where Hugo locked her in a room upstairs.

Downstairs, the men sat at a long table and began a wild feast, with loud songs and endless cups of wine. Hugo, who was greatly pleased with himself, did not think of the frightened girl above his head.
The girl, who had never been so afraid, tied together what she could find and climbed down the ivy under the window. She ran across the moor toward her father's farm, which was about nine miles away.

After a while Hugo takes food upstairs, and he finds the room empty and the bird gone. In a terrible rage he calls for his horse and looses his hounds, swearing to give his soul to evil if he can catch her.

The drunken men rode out after him, shouting and laughing, until they met a shepherd who was walking home across the moor. He told them in a shaking voice that he had seen the girl pass, and Hugo's black mare, with nobody on its back.

At last they find a lonely valley, and in it lies the girl, dead from fear and tiredness. Beside her lies Hugo, and over him stands a great black beast, larger than any hound men have seen, tearing at his throat.
Dr Mortimer ends with the writer's warning to his sons, never to cross the moor in the dark hours when evil is strong. He folds the paper carefully, and the room is quiet for a moment.

Holmes opens his eyes and says that the manuscript is an interesting fairy tale, but he asks what it has to do with today. Dr Mortimer answers by reading a newspaper cutting about the sudden death of Sir Charles Baskerville.

Mortimer explains that Sir Charles was a close friend of his and one of the kindest men he ever knew. He had earned a fortune abroad, returned to the Hall, and meant to spend his money on the poor of the district.

The old gentleman, however, had a weak heart, as Mortimer well knew, and in recent months he had grown nervous and easily frightened. He believed in the family curse more than he cared to admit, and he would not go out on the moor after dark.

Every evening after dinner he walks up and down the Yew Alley, a long path between two walls of dark trees, with a cigar. On the night he died he had told his butler that he would go to London the next day.

When Sir Charles did not return at the usual time, Barrymore the butler took a lantern and went to search for him. The hall door was open, and Barrymore followed the footprints of his master along the damp gravel of the path.

At the end of the alley a small gate leads out onto the moor, and Barrymore finds it standing open. On the ground lies the ash of Sir Charles's cigar, which shows that he stood waiting at the gate for five or ten minutes.

Mortimer is called at once, and he finds his old friend lying on his face with his arms stretched out. The body has no wound, but the face is so twisted that he hardly knows it, and the court says that the heart failed.

Mortimer then admits that he noticed something that nobody else had seen, for he looked at the ground with more care than the others. About twenty yards from the body, on the soft earth beside the path, there were footprints that did not belong to a man.

Holmes asks in a quiet voice whether they were the footprints of a man or of a woman. Mortimer lowers his voice almost to a whisper and answers, “Mr Holmes, they were the footprints of a gigantic hound.”

Mortimer says that he told nobody, because nobody would have believed him, and he is not a man who fears ghosts. But Sir Henry Baskerville, the last of the family, arrives from Canada tomorrow morning, and Mortimer asks what in the world he ought to do.

Holmes tells Dr Mortimer to take a cab to the station, meet Sir Henry and say nothing yet about the legend. Then he sits up all night with his pipe, and Watson goes to bed wondering what he will find.

At ten o'clock the next morning Dr Mortimer returns with a sturdy young man of about thirty, with dark eyes and black eyebrows. This is Sir Henry Baskerville, who looks like a man who has spent many years in the open air.

Sir Henry says that he has received a very odd letter that morning, and he lays an envelope on the table. It is addressed to him in rough printed letters at the Northumberland Hotel, although nobody except Dr Mortimer knew that he would stay there.

Holmes opens the envelope and finds a single sheet of paper, on which words cut from a newspaper have been pasted in a line. It says, “As you value your life or your reason keep away from the moor,” and only the last word has been written by hand.

Holmes puts the page beside a copy of yesterday's newspaper and shows that every word was cut from one of its leading articles. Watson is amazed, because the small curved cuts tell Holmes that the sender used a pair of short scissors and was in a great hurry.
Holmes then holds the paper close to his face, and for a moment he seems to notice something in the air. He says nothing about it, but Watson knows the look of a man who has found a thread to follow.

Sir Henry adds that something else has been bothering him, because a brand new brown boot has vanished from outside his hotel room. He had put both boots out to be cleaned, and one was gone, a boot that he had bought only the day before.

Dr Mortimer tells Sir Henry the legend of the hound, and Sir Henry listens with great seriousness but no fear. He says that no devil and no man alive will keep him from the home of his family, and he means every word.

Holmes agrees that Sir Henry is right to go, but he insists that he must never walk alone. Sir Henry and Mortimer leave for their hotel, and Holmes asks them to come back for lunch, then seizes his hat and calls for Watson.

They follow the two men down Regent Street, and suddenly Holmes points at a cab crawling along behind them. Inside is a man with a thick black beard and staring eyes, who whips his horse and is lost in the traffic.
Holmes does not hurry to the hotel, but takes Watson to a picture gallery in Bond Street for nearly two hours. He talks about nothing but art, and he will not even mention the man in the cab.

At the hotel they find Sir Henry shouting at the manager, for this time an old black boot has disappeared from outside his door. The poor manager promises to search the whole building, and the porters look at each other in alarm.

By the evening the new brown boot has returned, set neatly in the corridor, but the old black one is nowhere to be found. Holmes says that it is strange for a thief to steal one boot and give another back.

Back in Baker Street, Holmes rings for Cartwright, a sharp young messenger who is small, quick and never forgets an order. He tells the boy exactly what he wants, and Cartwright salutes smartly and runs out of the door.

Cartwright is to visit every hotel near Charing Cross and look through the waste-paper baskets. He is searching for the newspaper from which Sir Henry's letter was cut, because it must have been thrown away in a hurry.

Holmes also writes a telegram to the Hall, asking that it be given to Barrymore the butler and no one else. If Barrymore is truly in Devonshire, he cannot be the bearded man who followed Sir Henry through the streets of London.

A heavy knock sounds at the door, and a rough cabman with a clay pipe is shown in. He is John Clayton, the driver of the cab that followed Sir Henry, and he has come because Holmes sent word to the cab stand.

Clayton says that his passenger was a man with a black beard who waited near the hotel and told him to follow two gentlemen. When Holmes asks the stranger's name, the driver grins and says that the man told him he was Sherlock Holmes.

Holmes throws back his head and laughs, for he knows that he has been matched by a clever and daring enemy. Later he writes down everything they know, and he decides that the real danger waits not in London but on the moor.

Holmes explains that a very delicate case for a noble family keeps him in town, and he cannot leave London for a day or two. He therefore asks Watson to go to Devonshire with Sir Henry, never to leave him alone for a moment and to write every day.

On the platform at Paddington, Holmes takes Watson aside and gives him his last orders in a low voice. He must watch Sir Henry day and night, never let him walk on the moor alone after dark, and notice everyone who comes near him.

The train carries the three travellers west through long hours of green fields, red earth and little villages with grey church towers. Sir Henry presses his face to the window and cries out with joy, because he has not seen England for many years.

At last they step down at a tiny station in the middle of the country, where two soldiers stand guard with rifles in their hands. The travellers look at them in surprise, for such a sight is not usual in so quiet a place.

A soldier explains that a convict has escaped from the great prison at Princetown, which is not far away. The man's name is Selden, and he was sentenced for a terrible crime, so the police warn every house to lock its doors.

The carriage waits outside, and they drive for some miles through narrow lanes where high green banks and ferns brush against the wheels. The air is cool and sweet, and yet Watson cannot shake off a strange feeling that something is watching them.

Suddenly the banks fall away and the moor opens before them, a vast brown and grey country broken by black rocks. On a distant hill a soldier sits on a horse, as still as a statue, and Watson sees that the whole land is watched.

The carriage turns through two stone gateposts and rolls up a long avenue of ancient elm trees, whose branches meet above it like a tunnel. At the end of the drive the old house rises out of the gloom, and Sir Henry shivers.

A tall, pale man with a black beard stands at the open door, holding a lantern, and bows to Sir Henry with great respect. This is Barrymore, the butler, and beside him is his wife, a stout woman with a serious face, who takes the travellers' bags.

Dinner is served in a long dining room with a high ceiling and black oak walls, lit by a few small lamps. Portraits of dead Baskervilles look down from the walls, and Sir Henry confesses that the whole place feels like a house in a dream.

Watson goes to bed early, but he cannot sleep, for the great clock strikes every quarter hour and the wind moans in the chimney. In the middle of the night he hears a woman sobbing, and in the morning Mrs Barrymore has red eyes and a swollen face.

After breakfast Sir Henry stays indoors with the estate papers, so Watson takes a walk alone along the path to Grimpen. The moor is wide and silent, and the wind is cool on his face as he leaves the park behind.

He has gone about a mile when he hears quick footsteps, and a thin man in a straw hat comes running with a butterfly net. He introduces himself as Stapleton of Merripit House, and he says that Dr Mortimer pointed Watson out.

Stapleton carries a green box for his specimens, and he says that the moor is full of rare butterflies and moths. He adds that he once kept a school in the north of England, but his health was poor, so he came to Devonshire for quiet.

Suddenly Stapleton spots a rare butterfly and, with a cry of delight, runs straight out onto the Mire. Watson watches in horror as the naturalist jumps from tuft to tuft, and he expects to see him vanish into the green slime.

On the way home Watson passes a hillside covered with the circles of old stone huts, where people lived thousands of years ago. They look cold and empty, though a few still have a part of a roof, and he thinks that a man could easily hide there.

In his first report, Watson tells Holmes about the long silent moor, the soldiers who search it and the convict who is still free. He also mentions the strange sobbing in the night, which he cannot explain.

He then lists the people who live near the Hall and who might know something. They are the Stapletons at Merripit House, Dr Mortimer in Grimpen and an old man named Mr Frankland, who is famous for his lawsuits.

Their talk is soon interrupted, for Stapleton comes striding over the grass with a pale face and angry eyes. He takes his sister roughly by the arm and tells her to come away at once, and she obeys without a word.
Sir Henry, who has done nothing wrong, stares after them with his fists on his hips. He says that he wants to know what he has done to deserve such a look, but Watson cannot answer him.

The next morning Stapleton calls at the Hall with his hat in his hands and a humble face. He says that his sister is all he has in the world, and then he invites Sir Henry and Watson to dinner on Friday.

On Friday evening the two men cross the moor as the light fades, and they come to a low grey house among bent trees. It is Merripit House, and Watson thinks that it is the loneliest place he has ever seen.

Before dinner Stapleton shows them his collection, row after row of butterflies and moths pinned in glass cases. He speaks of his old school in the north, where he taught boys for many years before the work grew too hard for his health.

At the table Miss Stapleton says hardly a word, and she eats very little of her dinner. Watson notices that she glances at Sir Henry with a look of fear, while her brother laughs and talks as if nothing were wrong.

After dinner they walk home across the dark moor under a sky full of stars, and Sir Henry is silent and thoughtful. Suddenly a long, deep howl rolls over the hills, and both men stop at once, and Watson's hand goes to the revolver in his pocket.

One night Watson wakes to the sound of a soft footstep in the corridor, and he sees a thin light moving under his door. He opens it a little and sees Barrymore creeping by in his stockings, with a lighted candle in his hand.

Watson follows him quietly to the end of the passage, where there is a window that looks out over the moor. Barrymore stands there and holds the candle against the glass, then waits for a long time before he turns away.

In the morning Watson tells Sir Henry what he has seen, and the young man listens with a serious face. They agree that the butler must be watched, and that if he does it again they will ask him straight out why.

The next night they sit up in Sir Henry's room with the door open a few inches, and they wait for hours in the darkness. The great clock strikes one, then two, and Watson is nearly asleep when they hear a soft step in the passage.

They follow the sound in their stockings and find Barrymore in an empty room, holding a candle close to the window. Sir Henry bursts in and asks him what he is doing, and the poor man almost drops the light.

Barrymore is white and shaking, and at first he says it is nothing, only a private matter that he cannot explain. When Sir Henry presses him, he admits that the candle is a signal and that someone out on the moor is waiting for it.
Barrymore's wife appears in the doorway, weeping, and at last the truth comes out. The man on the moor is the convict Selden, her younger brother, and she cannot let him starve.

While they are talking, Watson glances out of the window and sees a tiny yellow light shining far off in the darkness. Sir Henry says that it is the convict's answer, and he decides that he will go out and catch the man himself.

They put on their coats, take their revolvers and hurry across the moor under a bright moon, with Barrymore showing them the way. They soon see a wild, bearded figure running among the rocks, and they chase him as fast as they can.

Selden is faster and knows the ground better, and he escapes into the darkness, leaving the two men gasping for breath. As Watson looks back, he sees a tall, thin figure standing perfectly still on top of a high rock, black against the moon.

The next morning Barrymore thanks them for not handing Selden to the police, and he says that the man will soon leave for South America. Sir Henry, who has softened a little, gives the butler a bundle of old clothes for the convict.

Barrymore adds something that makes Watson think of the figure on the rock, for Selden says that another man is hiding on the moor. Selden does not know who the stranger is, but he thinks that he is a spy, and he is afraid.

Barrymore then confides that, after Sir Charles died, he found a piece of burned paper in the study fireplace. Only a few words are left, asking the reader to burn the letter and be at the gate at ten, signed L L.

Watson and Sir Henry show the scrap to Dr Mortimer, who thinks for a moment and then says that it must mean Laura Lyons. She lives in Coombe Tracey, and she is the daughter of Mr Frankland, who has not spoken to her since she married an artist.
Watson sets out for Coombe Tracey at once, and on the way he passes Lafter Hall, where an old man waves a stick. This is Mr Frankland, and he talks about his lawsuits as if they were great victories.

Mr Frankland takes Watson up onto his flat roof and shows him a large brass telescope pointed at the moor. He says that he spends his days watching for the escaped convict, and he can see the Hall's gates from there.

At Coombe Tracey a servant shows Watson into a small, neat sitting room, where a lady sits at a table beside a typewriter. Laura Lyons is slim and graceful, with dark eyes and soft red hair, but she looks at him with a careful and anxious face.

Watson says that he knows about the burned letter, and Laura Lyons twists her handkerchief and admits that she wrote it. She says that she was in great trouble and needed money to free herself from her husband, so she begged Sir Charles for help.

She says that she asked him to meet her at the gate on the night he died, but she never went there. She also admits that she wrote the words about burning the letter, because she did not want anyone to know about her trouble.

Watson asks why she stayed away, and she answers only that a friend advised her not to go. When he asks the friend's name, she shakes her head and refuses, and Watson leaves feeling sure that she is hiding something important.

On the way home Frankland calls Watson back up to his roof and points the telescope at a distant hill. He says that for several days a boy has carried food to the same rocky tor, and he thinks it is for the convict.

Back at the Hall, Sir Henry says that he is invited to dine at Merripit House that evening and wants to go. Watson decides to climb the tor at once, because he thinks he can be back in good time to walk with him.

The path to the tor is steep and stony, and the afternoon is hot and quiet. Watson climbs slowly with his hand on his revolver, and from the top he sees a wide sweep of empty moor where nothing moves.

On the summit he finds a ring of old stone huts, and one of them still has half a roof. Inside he sees a rolled blanket, several tins of food, an empty bottle and a few cigarette ends, so someone has been living here comfortably.

On a flat stone beside the blanket lies a half-sheet of paper, and Watson picks it up with a cold feeling in his stomach. It is written in a neat small hand, and it says that Dr Watson has gone to Coombe Tracey, so someone has been following him.

Watson stands and listens, and from somewhere outside he hears the click of a boot on the stones. He crouches in a dark corner with his revolver ready, and then a long shadow falls across the doorway of the hut.

“It's a lovely evening, my dear Watson,” says a familiar voice, “and I really think that you will be more comfortable outside than in.” Watson gasps, because in the doorway, smiling and calm, stands Sherlock Holmes.

Holmes explains that he never really stayed in London, and that he came down in secret to see the moor with his own eyes. If he had arrived openly, he says, the enemy would have been warned, so he has been living in this old hut for several days.
Holmes tells Watson that the tall man on the rock was himself, and that the boy with the food is Cartwright. He also says that he read Watson's reports every day, and that they were very useful.
Watson tells Holmes about Laura Lyons, and Holmes listens closely and nods. Then he asks where Sir Henry is, and when Watson says that he is dining at Merripit House, Holmes springs to his feet.
Holmes and Watson hurry down the hill as the sun sinks behind the moor and the shadows grow long. Holmes says very little as they go, but Watson can see by his face that he is worried.

They follow a narrow path toward Merripit House, and the sky grows dark above them while the first stars appear. Holmes tells Watson in a low voice that he fears for Sir Henry's walk home that night, and he checks his revolver.
They are still some distance from the house when a terrible scream breaks the silence, a high cry of terror and pain. Holmes stops as though he has been struck, and his hand shakes on Watson's arm.

They run toward the sound over the dark and uneven ground, but the cry has already died away, and the moor is silent again. Then, far off, comes a long deep howl, and Watson feels his heart turn cold.
They hurry on and come to a group of rocks, and at the bottom of the slope they see a dark shape on the ground. It is a man lying face downward, with his head bent under him at a terrible angle.

Holmes strikes a match and holds it above the body, and its small flame shows a pale face with a thick black beard. Watson recognises him at once, and he cries out that it is Selden, the convict who escaped from Princetown.

The dead man wears a tweed suit that Watson knows well, because Sir Henry gave it to Barrymore for his brother-in-law. Holmes sees at once what this means, and he understands why the hound chased the wrong man.

They search the slope and the rocks all around, and Holmes even listens for the sound of heavy paws. But they find no trace of any animal, and the only sound is a faint howl that grows weaker and then disappears.
They are still standing beside the body when they hear a quick step, and a thin man comes out of the darkness. It is Stapleton, and he asks in a nervous voice whether Sir Henry is hurt.

Stapleton suddenly sees Holmes beside the body, and he looks as if he has seen a ghost. Holmes calmly introduces himself, and Watson notices that when Stapleton looks down at the dead man, his face shows something more like disappointment than grief.

Stapleton asks how the man died, and Holmes tells him that Selden fell from the rocks while he was running in the dark. The naturalist says that he is sorry, and he promises to send word to the police.

When Stapleton has gone, Holmes whispers to Watson that the naturalist asked first about Sir Henry, and that he showed no grief for the convict. It is a small thing, says Holmes, but a clever man notices small things.

At dawn Holmes and Watson walk to the Hall, where Sir Henry is eating breakfast with a pale and puzzled face. He jumps up with a cry of joy and surprise at the sight of Holmes, and the two men shake hands warmly.

Holmes tells Barrymore gently that Selden is dead, and the butler bows his head and says nothing for a long time. Mrs Barrymore cries quietly in the kitchen, and Sir Henry promises that the poor man will have a proper burial.

That afternoon Holmes asks to be shown the gallery, and he walks slowly down the long dark room with a lamp in his hand. He stops before each portrait, and at last he stands for a long time in front of Hugo Baskerville, in his hat and curls.

Holmes puts his hand over the cavalier's hat and long hair, and then he stands back and looks at the face. Watson looks too, and suddenly he sees the thin, sharp features of Stapleton looking back at him out of the painting.

Holmes explains that the face in the picture has come down through the family, and that Stapleton must be a Baskerville by blood. He says that this is the key to everything, and it shows that Stapleton has a reason to want the estate.

The next morning Holmes and Watson drive to Coombe Tracey and call on Laura Lyons, who looks frightened to see two visitors. Holmes tells her politely that he knows she did not tell Watson the whole truth, and that he will put it before her.

Holmes says that the man she calls a friend is Stapleton, and that the lady with him is his wife, not his sister. Laura Lyons covers her face with her hands, because Stapleton had promised to marry her.

At last she tells the truth: Stapleton himself told her what to write to Sir Charles, and then told her to stay at home. That evening a small, sallow man in a brown suit steps off the train, and Holmes greets Inspector Lestrade with a smile.

That evening in the library, Holmes explains his plan to Sir Henry and Lestrade, and he draws a map on a sheet of paper. The hound will only be caught if Stapleton believes that he can still hurt Sir Henry, and for that Sir Henry must be the bait.

Sir Henry listens with a steady face and then agrees without a moment's doubt, though Watson can see that his hands are not quite still. He will go to Merripit House for dinner, and he will walk home across the moor alone.
Holmes lets it be known that he and Watson are called back to London, so that Stapleton will think the way is clear. He also tells Sir Henry to keep to the path and never to run toward the Mire.

At dusk on the night of the dinner, Holmes, Watson and Lestrade walk out onto the moor with revolvers in their pockets. Lestrade, a small, tough man who has chased criminals all over London, grumbles at the dark but follows.
Holmes leads them to a pile of tall rocks about two hundred yards from Merripit House, where they can see the lamplit windows. They crouch behind the stones, and the night grows cold around them.

While they wait, Holmes looks across the moor and sees a long, low line of white mist rising slowly from the Grimpen Mire. He mutters that the fog is a danger, because it could hide the path completely, and he looks worried.

The mist grows thicker and moves closer, and soon it swirls around the rocks in cold white clouds. Holmes lies down with his ear to the ground, listens for a moment, and then moves the three men nearer to the path.

The lights of Merripit House shine pale and yellow through the fog, and the hours seem to pass very slowly. Nobody speaks, and Watson counts the beats of his own heart as the night grows later and later.
At last the door of the house opens, and a stream of lamplight falls upon the grass. Sir Henry steps out, says good night, and begins to walk along the path with a firm step and a cheerful whistle.

Holmes grips Lestrade's wrist and whispers to them to be ready, while the fog rolls over the whole path like a great wall. Then, out of the white darkness, Watson hears a soft pattering sound, like the paws of a heavy animal.

Sir Henry passes within a few yards of the rocks, whistling and looking straight ahead, quite unaware of the men beside the path. Holmes holds his breath and tells the others not to move until he gives the signal.
Then, out of the fog behind him, springs the most terrible creature that Watson has ever seen. It is a huge coal-black hound, as big as a small lion, and its mouth and eyes glow with a hellish fire.
The hound bounds past the rocks, and all three men fire at once, and Watson hears a howl as a shot hits it. But the beast races on along the path after the young man.

Sir Henry hears the noise and turns, and when he sees the great shape rushing at him, he screams in terror and starts to run. The hound is too fast for him, and it leaps upon his back and throws him to the ground.

Holmes runs forward like a madman and fires five shots into the creature's side, one after another. The hound gives a last great howl, rolls over in the grass, kicks wildly for a moment with its paws, and then lies still.

Sir Henry lies faint upon the grass, and Holmes bends over him and finds that he is alive and unhurt. The huge dog lies beside him, quite dead, and there is a pale blue light shining about its muzzle.

Holmes touches the glowing mouth and holds up his hand, and Watson sees that his fingers are shining in the dark. It is a chemical called phosphorus, and Holmes says that whoever put it on the dog meant to frighten his victims to death.

Watson pours some brandy from a flask between Sir Henry's lips, and the young man opens his eyes and stares around in confusion. Holmes tells him gently that the monster is only a dog, and that the terror of the family is dead.

Lestrade, who has recovered from his astonishment, stays beside the dead hound, and Holmes and Watson hurry to Merripit House. The front door stands open, and they search the dark rooms, but they find no sign of Stapleton.

At last they hear a faint thumping from upstairs, and in a bedroom they find a woman tied to a post with strips of sheet. It is Beryl Stapleton, and Holmes quickly unties her and gives her a drink of water.

When Beryl has recovered a little, Holmes asks her gently who she is, and she says in a low voice that she is Stapleton's wife. He made her pretend to be his sister, because he said that it would help his plans.

She tells them that Stapleton ran off into the Mire when he saw that the hound was dead. He has a secret path across the bog that is marked with white sticks, and it leads to an island where he used to hide.

Holmes and Watson carry Sir Henry to Merripit House and lay him on a sofa, while the fog presses against the windows. It is impossible to follow anyone across the Mire in such darkness, so they wait for the morning.

At dawn the fog begins to thin, and the sun shows a wide, silent bog, bright green and quiet in the pale light. Beryl shows them the place where the secret path begins, and Holmes thanks her warmly for her help.

Holmes, Watson and Lestrade follow the white sticks one by one, stepping carefully on the firm tufts and keeping away from the black pools. The ground trembles and sucks at their boots, and Watson does not dare to think what would happen if he slipped.
In the middle of the bog they find an island with the ruins of an old mine and an iron stake with a chain. Around it lies a heap of bones, and the place smells of dog, so it was the hound's den.

As they walk back along the path, Holmes stops and bends down, and he picks up an old black boot half buried in the mud. He turns it over and says that it is the boot that was stolen from Sir Henry's hotel.

Holmes explains that the thief first took a new boot, which has no scent, so he returned it and took an old one. Stapleton let the hound smell this old boot, and that is how it learned to hunt Sir Henry.

They follow the path to its end, where the white sticks stop, and they see footprints that lead to a pool of green slime. It looks as though Stapleton lost the path in the fog and stepped into the mud.
They search the edges of the bog for many hours, but there is no sign of him. Holmes stands looking at the still green water and says quietly that the Mire never gives up what it takes.
Some days later, with Sir Henry strong enough to sit up, the four men gather round the great fire, and Holmes lights his pipe. He says that he will explain the case in its proper order.

First, he says, the man they knew as Stapleton was really a Baskerville, the son of Rodger Baskerville, who was Sir Charles's younger brother. It was this family blood that Holmes saw in the old portrait, and it explains why Stapleton wanted the estate.

Rodger, says Holmes, was the black sheep of the family, who left England in disgrace and died of fever in Central America. Everyone believed that he died unmarried and without children, but they were wrong.

Rodger had in fact married, and his son grew up to become a schoolmaster in the north of England, where he used a different name. When one of his pupils died of a fever, the school failed, and he left in a hurry to try his luck elsewhere.

The man changed his name to Stapleton and moved south with his wife Beryl, a beautiful girl whom he had married in Costa Rica. He loved his butterflies, and the study of them gave him a good reason to come to the quiet moors of Devonshire.

In Devonshire, Holmes continues, Stapleton learned that only two lives stood between him and the great Baskerville fortune. They were the old, childless Sir Charles, who had a weak heart, and the young heir who was living in Canada.
Holmes turns kindly to Dr Mortimer and says that he is not to blame for telling his neighbour about the old legend. A clever, wicked mind could use such innocent talk very well.

Stapleton decided that the legend would be his tool, so he bought a huge dog in London, part mastiff and part bloodhound. He brought it secretly to the moor by train, and he hid it in an old tin mine in the Mire.
To make the dog look like a ghost, Stapleton rubbed phosphorus onto its coat and muzzle, so that it shone in the dark. He trained the animal with great patience to hunt, and it obeyed him.

Then he needed to bring Sir Charles to the moor gate at night, and for that he used Laura Lyons. He told her what to write, and he promised to marry her, and Sir Charles went to the gate on the fatal evening.
Holmes tells how Sir Charles waited at the gate for a lady who never came, because Stapleton had kept her at home. Instead, out of the darkness, the great glowing hound came bounding toward him.

Sir Charles, who had a weak heart, turned and ran for his life down the avenue of yew trees. Mortimer remembers that the marks showed a man running on his toes, and his heart gave way before the hound touched him.

Stapleton, says Holmes, then called off his hound and went home, quite sure that no one could prove anything against him. No court in England, he thought, would believe that a dog could be the murderer of a man.

When Sir Henry came from Canada, Stapleton and his wife followed him to London, where they stayed at a small hotel and watched him. Stapleton put on a black beard, and that is how he hired the cab and followed the young man.

Holmes then reveals that it was Beryl who secretly sent the warning letter, cutting the words from the newspaper because she feared for Sir Henry. Holmes noticed a faint scent of white jessamine on the paper, and he knew that a lady had been involved.
A hotel servant, says Holmes, was paid by Stapleton to take the boots. A new boot was no use to a hound, so he took an old one, and Holmes found it later in the Mire.

Stapleton had meant to use Beryl's charm to bring Sir Henry to Merripit, but she refused to help him hurt the young man. When Sir Henry began to love her, her husband grew jealous and furious, and that was the reason for his rage on the moor.

On the night of the scream, Sir Henry's old clothes caused Selden's death, because the hound followed their scent. The poor convict ran blindly in the dark, fell from a rock and died, and the hound ran on.

Holmes frowns and admits that he took a great risk when he used Sir Henry as bait, and that things might have gone wrong. But he says that no jury would have believed the story of a ghostly dog without a real one before their eyes.
At last Holmes finishes his story and leans back in his chair, and for a time no one speaks. The only sound in the great hall is the slow ticking of the old clock, and then it strikes twelve.

A few days later Sir Henry still wakes at night, shaking from his terrible experience, and Dr Mortimer examines him carefully. The doctor says that he needs a long rest and a sea voyage, and Sir Henry agrees to travel with him around the world.

Selden is buried in the quiet churchyard at Grimpen on a grey morning, and only a few people stand beside the grave. Barrymore holds his hat in his hands, and his wife, who has cried so many nights, is at last calm.

Soon afterward Barrymore comes to Sir Henry with his cap in his hands and says that he and his wife wish to leave. Sir Charles left them a little money, and they want to start a small business of their own, far from the moor.

Mr Frankland arrives at the Hall one day, as red-faced and cheerful as ever, and he claims that his telescope helped to solve the mystery. Holmes listens with a polite smile, and he thanks the old man for his help.
Lestrade thinks that Laura Lyons should be arrested, but Holmes shakes his head. He explains that she was tricked by a clever man who promised her marriage, and that she knew nothing of any danger.

Beryl gives her statement to the police and is allowed to go, and she leaves the moor on a quiet morning with one small bag. She wants to live in peace somewhere far away, and she thanks Holmes for believing her.

Sir Henry, who is feeling stronger, walks through the great hall and throws open the tall windows so that the sunlight pours in. He says that he will fill the old house with light and with friends, as his uncle always meant to do.

On their last night at the Hall, Holmes and Watson walk down the Yew Alley to the little gate on the moor. The moon is bright, the moor is silent, and for the first time Watson feels that it is only a lonely and beautiful place.

Sir Henry gives a farewell dinner, and he stands to thank Holmes and Watson for saving his life. He says that he will never forget the cold night on the moor, and that he is proud to have such friends.

The next morning the trunks stand in the hall, and the house is full of the noise of packing and goodbyes. Sir Henry, who is pale but smiling, shakes hands with each of the servants before he goes outside.
On the steps of the old house, Sir Henry shakes Holmes's hand and promises to return when he has seen the world. He says that the next time they meet, the Hall will be full of light and music.

The carriage rolls down the long avenue of elms and along the road past Merripit House, which stands shuttered and silent among its trees. Holmes does not look at it, but Watson sees a curtain move, and he turns away.
As they climb a hill, Watson looks back at the bright, quiet moor, with purple heather rolling toward the far tors. It seems impossible that such a lovely place could have held such terror.

At the station, Sir Henry and Dr Mortimer take a different train toward the port, where their ship waits. The doctor's spaniel jumps up beside them, and they wave from the window until the train turns the corner.

Lestrade shakes hands with Holmes and admits that he will never forget the sight of the glowing hound as long as he lives. Then he tips his hat, picks up his bag, and says that the Yard will hear of this for years.

Holmes and Watson sit facing each other in the rattling carriage and talk over the case from beginning to end. Holmes explains the small points once again, and Watson is amazed at how many clues he missed.

Holmes smiles and looks out at the flying green fields, and he remarks that it has been one of the strangest cases of his life. He says that the world is full of clever villains, but few of them would have used a dog.

They reach London after dark, and a heavy yellow fog hangs over the streets and turns every lamp to a blurred ball of light. A cab takes them slowly through the crowds, and Watson finds that the noise of the city feels like a welcome.

At Baker Street the good Mrs Hudson meets them at the door and hurries to bring them tea and a hot supper. Holmes sinks into his old armchair, stretches his feet toward the bright fire, and sighs with deep pleasure.

Later that evening Holmes puts down his pipe and says with a smile that he has two tickets for the opera. Watson laughs, glad to see his friend relaxed again after so many days of danger, and they put on their coats together.

He waited, with some satisfaction and a little impatience, for his friend to praise the reasoning and to admit that it was sound.

Dr Mortimer twisted his long hands together and admitted that he was a practical man of science, who had never believed in ghosts or curses. Yet he was now caught in a matter so strange and so frightening that he had lain awake for several nights, unable to decide what to do.

Holmes leaned back in his chair, closed his eyes and joined his fingertips, the attitude in which he was always at his most attentive. Dr Mortimer drew a yellowed manuscript from his coat, smoothed it carefully on his knee and cleared his throat in a way that promised a long reading. In a high, cracking voice he began, and the morning light seemed to grow a little colder as the old words filled the room.

Dr Mortimer explained that the paper was a family chronicle, written in the year 1742 by a Baskerville who wished to warn his two young sons of a danger he did not understand. The author had received the tale from his own father, who had had it in turn from his, so that it had passed down the generations like a dark inheritance. Holmes, who had not once opened his eyes, murmured that the doctor might continue, and the doctor, clearing his throat, did so.

According to the old writer, the Hall in the time of the Civil War had belonged to a man named Hugo Baskerville, who was godless, violent and without any wish to be loved. His neighbours shunned him, his servants trembled at the sound of his voice, and the chronicle admitted frankly that no good word had ever been said of him in all the countryside. Such a man, it observed, was bound sooner or later to meet his match.

That match was a farmer's daughter, a quiet and modest girl, who unluckily attracted the squire's attention one autumn and could not escape it. She had heard enough of his reputation to avoid him like a plague, crossing the road when he approached and lowering her eyes whenever he spoke. Her coldness only fed his stubborn desire, as such coldness often does in men of his sort.

On a certain dark night, Hugo and five or six of his wildest companions crept up to the farm when the girl's father and brothers had gone away. They seized her, dragged her to the Hall and shut her in a chamber at the top of the house, while they went below to enjoy a victory. It was a shameful deed, and the old chronicler did not trouble to pretend otherwise.

Down in the great hall the company sat at table with their cups, roaring out songs, shouting toasts and growing wilder with every hour of the night. Hugo, flushed with wine and triumph, had quite forgotten that the prisoner above him was a living, frightened girl. Not one of the men, it seems, spared a single thought for the frightened girl locked in the room above their heads.

Meanwhile the girl, driven by terror, tore her clothes into strips, tied them together and lowered herself from the window along the thick ivy that clung to the wall. Dropping to the ground, she fled across the moor in the darkness, for her father's farm lay nine miles away. Behind her, the lights of the Hall dwindled and the great silence of the moor closed in.

When Hugo at last carried food and drink up to his prisoner, he found the room empty and the window open to the night, and his rage was terrible to see. He rushed down to the hall, shouted for his black mare and, flinging open the kennels, set his hounds upon the girl's scent. Swearing a great oath that he would give his soul to the powers of evil if he could overtake her, he galloped out after the hounds into the night.

The drunken revellers, stunned for a moment, snatched up their horses and followed him, their hoofbeats ringing over the moorland. Presently they met a shepherd, who stood trembling beside the road, and when they asked whether he had seen the hunt, he answered in a voice that was scarcely human. He had seen the girl flying past, with Hugo's hounds in pursuit, and then Hugo's black mare, foaming and riderless, and behind her something that no man should ever look upon.

Sobered at last, the company rode on until they came to a lonely valley, where the moonlight lay cold upon the grass. There they found the poor girl, who had died of fear and exhaustion, and near her the body of Hugo Baskerville, and over him stood a monstrous black hound with burning eyes. It was larger than any hound ever seen and was tearing at his throat, and one of the riders is said to have died of fright that very night, while the rest were broken men for life.

The chronicle closed with a plea to the writer's sons to keep away from the moor in those dark hours when the powers of evil are exalted, and Dr Mortimer read the last line slowly, as though weighing it. Then he folded the yellow pages, laid them on his knee and looked round at the two men. The room had become oddly still, and even the ticking of the clock seemed softer than before.

Holmes opened his eyes and observed, with a little weariness, that the manuscript made a pleasant fairy tale but that he failed to see its bearing on a case of the present day. Dr Mortimer, as though he had expected the remark, drew a newspaper cutting from his pocket and smoothed it on his knee. It was an account of the sudden death of Sir Charles Baskerville, which had taken place only a few months before and had startled the whole of Devonshire.

Mortimer described his dead friend as one of the kindest and most open-handed men he had ever known, a man who had made a fortune abroad and returned to the old Hall with the plan of spending it well. Sir Charles meant to repair the estate, to give work to the poor of the district and to end his days among his own people. It was a worthy dream, and the doctor spoke of it with a trace of sorrow in his voice.

Yet the old gentleman's heart, as the doctor knew only too well, had been weak for years, and in the last months of his life he had grown strangely nervous and easily alarmed. He had come to believe, more deeply than he would admit, in the curse of his house, and nothing could have persuaded him to walk out upon the moor after dark. A shadow seemed to follow him even in his own rooms, and he started at every sound in the silent old house.

It was his habit, after dinner, to stroll up and down the Yew Alley, a long path enclosed between two thick walls of dark trees, with a cigar between his lips. On the night of his death he had told his butler that he would travel to London the next day, and he had gone out as usual into the cool evening air. Nothing in his manner, however, had warned the household of what was coming, and no one thought to follow him.

When the old man had not returned at his usual hour, Barrymore the butler lit a lantern and went in search of him, with a growing unease that he could not explain. The hall door stood open, and by the light of his lamp he followed his master's footprints along the damp gravel until he reached the far end of the path. It was a lonely walk through the whispering trees, and his heart must have beaten quickly as he went.

At the end of the alley there is a small wooden gate that opens onto the moor, and Barrymore found it standing wide in the darkness. On the ground beside it lay a little heap of grey ash from a cigar, which showed plainly that Sir Charles had stood there, smoking and waiting, for some five or ten minutes. What he had been waiting for at that lonely gate, in the middle of the night, nobody could say.

Mortimer was sent for at once, and he found his old friend lying face downward, with his arms outstretched and his fingers dug into the earth. There was not a wound or a bruise upon the body, but the face was so distorted that the doctor could scarcely recognise it, and the inquest returned a verdict that the heart had failed under some sudden strain. It was a calm decision, but it did not satisfy the one man who had seen everything.

Mortimer then confessed that he had noticed what no one else had thought to look for, because he had studied the ground around the body with more care than the rest. About twenty yards away from it, on the soft earth at the side of the path, he had found a line of footprints that clearly were not the prints of any man. He had said nothing at the time, and the thought of them had haunted him ever since.

Holmes, who was now sitting bolt upright, asked in a voice of studied calm whether the tracks had been made by a man or by a woman. Dr Mortimer lowered his voice until it was almost a whisper, and answered, “Mr Holmes, they were the footprints of a gigantic hound.” For a moment not even the clock in the corner seemed to breathe, and the room waited in a strange, heavy silence.

The doctor added that he had told no one, because no one would have believed him, and that he was neither fanciful nor easily frightened. But the last of the Baskervilles, Sir Henry, was to arrive from Canada by the morning train the very next day, and the doctor had to decide what to do with him. He begged Holmes, in plain words, to tell him how a sensible man ought to act.

Holmes advised the doctor to take a cab to the station, to meet Sir Henry as arranged and to say nothing whatever about the legend until the next day. When their visitor had gone, he filled his pipe, lay back on the sofa and sat up through the whole of the night, so that by morning the room was dim with smoke. Watson, who knew the signs, went to bed wondering what thread his friend was following in that grey haze.

At ten o'clock the following morning Dr Mortimer returned, bringing with him a sturdy young man of about thirty, dark-eyed and heavy-browed, whose face had been browned by many winds. This was Sir Henry Baskerville, who had just crossed an ocean to take up his inheritance, and he looked far more at home out of doors than in the drawing rooms of London. He shook hands with a firm, frank grip and sat down with the air of a man who preferred plain speech.

He said that he had received a very curious letter that morning, and with a puzzled frown he laid an envelope on the table. It was addressed in rough printed capitals to the Northumberland Hotel, though nobody except Dr Mortimer had known that he would choose to stay there. The postmark, as Holmes quickly noted, said Charing Cross, and the letter had been posted the evening before.

Holmes slit the envelope and drew out a half sheet of paper, on which a line of printed words had been pasted neatly, one after another. It said, “As you value your life or your reason keep away from the moor,” and only the last word, the one about the moor, had been written in ink by hand.
