The message was short, but it carried a shadow of menace that seemed to spread through the room.

Spreading the page beside a copy of the previous day's newspaper, Holmes demonstrated that every word had been cut from one of its leading articles, with the small, curved snips that only short scissors could make. He pointed out, with something like pleasure, that the hurried cutting told its own story and that the sender had acted in a great rush. Watson could only wonder at how a few scraps of paper could be made to give up so many secrets.

Then, almost carelessly, Holmes raised the letter to his face and drew in a slow breath, as though some faint perfume lingered upon it. Watson saw his friend's eyes narrow, and he knew that the great detective had noticed something that the others had missed, though not a word was spoken. It was one of those quiet moments when Holmes held his thoughts close and let the evidence do the speaking later.

Sir Henry then admitted that a smaller mystery was annoying him even more than the letter, for one of his new brown boots had disappeared from outside his hotel room. He had bought the pair only the day before in the Strand, had set them out to be cleaned and had found that one of them was gone before he had even worn it. It was a trifling loss, he said, but it had put him out of temper for the entire morning.

When Dr Mortimer, with obvious reluctance, repeated the story of the Hound, Sir Henry heard it out in silence and then declared that nothing on earth would prevent him from going to the home of his ancestors. He said it without bravado, as a man states a fact, and there was something so steady in his square, honest face that Watson felt a sudden liking for him. Holmes, however, sat frowning at the fire, as though he heard in those brave words something that the young man did not.

Holmes admitted that Sir Henry was right to go, since the place was his own, but he insisted firmly that he must never be left to walk alone upon the moor. The two visitors rose to return to their hotel, and Holmes asked them to come back for lunch, then waited until they were gone, snatched up his hat and called to Watson to follow. His face had the look of a hound that has caught the scent, and Watson hurried after him.

They kept the two men in sight as they went down Regent Street, and then, without warning, Holmes seized his friend's sleeve and pointed to a cab that was crawling along the kerb a little way behind. Inside it sat a man with a thick black beard and bright, fierce eyes, who shouted to his driver, and the cab dashed away through the crowded street. By the time Holmes had hailed another cab and given chase, the bearded man had vanished into the London traffic.

To Watson's surprise, Holmes did not hurry back to the hotel, but strolled into a picture gallery in Bond Street and spent nearly two hours gazing at the work of the Belgian painters. He talked of colour and form with a relish that seemed almost strange in the midst of such a chase, and he would not allow a single word about the black-bearded man to pass his lips. It was his way, as Watson well knew, of letting the mind rest while the hidden machinery went on working.

When at last they reached the Northumberland Hotel, they found Sir Henry pacing the hall in a fury, for this time an old black boot had vanished from outside his door. The unhappy manager promised to search the whole building from cellar to roof, and the porters hurried about with anxious faces, but nothing was found. Sir Henry's temper, which had been rising all day, grew hotter with every excuse.

By the evening the new brown boot had been quietly returned to the corridor, set neatly where it had first stood, as if nothing had happened, but the old black one remained missing. Holmes pointed out that it was an odd thing for any thief to steal a boot, give it back and then take another, and he stored the thought away in his mind. A small, absurd mystery was beginning to look like part of a larger plan.

Back in the rooms at Baker Street, Holmes rang for Cartwright, a small, quick-witted boy who ran errands for him across London and had never been known to forget an instruction. He gave the lad his orders in a few clear words, and the boy, who would have walked into a fire for his master, saluted and darted away down the stairs. It seemed a modest beginning to what was fast becoming a grave and dangerous affair, but Holmes knew that great matters often turn on small ones.

Cartwright was to visit every hotel near Charing Cross, ask politely to look through the waste-paper baskets and hunt for the newspaper from which Sir Henry's warning had been cut. Holmes reasoned that the sender, in his hurry, would have thrown the damaged page away, and that its discovery would show where the man had been staying. It was a long chance, but Holmes was fond of such chances, since the great successes of his career had often hung upon them.

Holmes also wrote out a telegram addressed to the Hall in Devonshire, with a request that it be handed to Barrymore the butler in person and to nobody else. If the reply proved that Barrymore was at his post, he could not have been the bearded stranger who had followed Sir Henry through the London streets that morning. It was a neat way of crossing one name from a short list of suspects.

That evening a heavy knock sounded at the door, and a rough, red-faced cabman with a clay pipe in his mouth was shown into the room. He was John Clayton, the driver of the very cab that had pursued Sir Henry, and he had come in answer to a message that Holmes had left at the stand where the cab's number was known. He turned his hat in his hands, plainly wondering what he had done wrong.

Clayton told them that his passenger had been a man with a black beard, who had waited close to the hotel and then ordered him to follow two gentlemen. When Holmes asked whether the man had given a name, the cabman grinned and said that he had, and that it was Sherlock Holmes. The great detective threw back his head and laughed until the tears came into his eyes, for his enemy had borrowed his own name.

The laughter faded as quickly as it had come, and Holmes sat silent for some time, with his chin sunk upon his chest, considering the cleverness and the nerve of the man who had so boldly used his name. Then he took paper and wrote down all that they knew, the letter, the boots, the cab and the telegram, and the sum of it all pointed in one direction. The danger, he told Watson, would not be found in London but out on the lonely moor.

Holmes explained that a very delicate case for a noble family held him in town, and that to leave London in the middle of it would be quite impossible. He therefore proposed that Watson should go to Devonshire with Sir Henry, never let the young man out of his sight, and write him a full report every day. Watson, who had never refused his friend anything, agreed at once, and Sir Henry shook his hand with delight.

On the platform at Paddington, as the engine hissed and the guard walked along slamming doors, Holmes drew his friend aside and spoke to him in a low and urgent voice. Watson was to keep Sir Henry in sight every hour of the day and night, was never to allow him upon the moor after dark, and was to take careful note of everyone who came near him. It was the gravest charge that the detective had ever laid upon him, and Watson promised to carry it out to the letter.

The train bore the three travellers westward through long hours of rolling green country, past little villages with grey church towers and fields of rich red earth. Sir Henry, who had not seen his native land since he was a boy, sat with his face pressed to the window, and from time to time he cried out with pleasure at a hill or a farm. Even Dr Mortimer's spaniel seemed to share his delight, as it stood with its paws upon the seat.

At last the train drew up at a tiny station with white railings, and on the platform they were surprised to see two soldiers in uniform standing guard with their rifles. No one had warned them of the sight, and the contrast between such stern figures and the sleepy country scene struck Watson as sinister. Even the porter, who carried their luggage to the waiting carriage, glanced often over his shoulder as though he feared to be overheard.

One of the soldiers explained, with a grave and civil air, that a convict had escaped from the great prison at Princetown and was believed to be hiding somewhere on the moor. His name was Selden, and he had been condemned for a savage crime, and the police had warned every farm and cottage in the district to keep its doors barred at night. For the first time Watson understood why the countryside seemed so silent and watchful.

The carriage was waiting outside, and they drove for several miles along narrow lanes, with high green banks on either side and ferns brushing against the wheels. The air was cool and sweet, the fields were bright with the last of the sun, and yet Watson could not shake off a curious feeling that unseen eyes were following them. He told himself that it was only the effect of the soldiers and the legend.

Without warning, the banks fell away on either hand and the moor lay open before them, a vast, bleak land of brown and grey, broken here and there by jagged black rocks. On the crest of a distant hill, a mounted soldier sat as motionless as a statue against the sky, his rifle across his saddle. The sight brought home to Watson how great an anxiety the escaped prisoner had become, and how closely the whole country was watched.

Presently the carriage turned between two weather-beaten stone gateposts and rolled up a long avenue of ancient elms, whose branches met overhead like the roof of a dark tunnel. At the end of the drive the old house rose out of the gathering dusk, grey and silent, with a few lights in its windows. Sir Henry shivered and remarked that it was small wonder his uncle had felt trouble coming in such a gloomy place.

On the threshold stood a tall, pale man with a black beard, holding a lantern, who bowed to the new master with the grave courtesy of a servant of the old school. This was Barrymore, the butler, and at his side stood his wife, a stout, sober woman, who took the travellers' bags in silence and led the way into the great hall. Watson noticed that her hands were not quite steady, and that her eyes avoided the faces of the strangers.

Dinner was served in a long, high dining room panelled in black oak, which two or three small lamps could scarcely light, and where the shadows seemed to crowd round the table. Portraits of dead Baskervilles stared down from the walls with an air of faded pride, and Sir Henry admitted in a whisper that the house felt like a place in a bad dream. Watson, glancing up at the dark minstrels' gallery, where the shadows gathered thickest, could not honestly disagree with him.

Weary as he was, Watson lay awake for hours that night, listening to the great clock below strike every quarter and to the wind moaning in the chimney. Somewhere in the small hours he heard, quite clearly, the sound of a woman sobbing, a low, broken, hopeless sound that seemed to come from within the house itself. At breakfast Mrs Barrymore's eyes were red and her face swollen, and Watson wondered what sorrow lay behind her silence.

After breakfast Sir Henry shut himself up with the estate papers, and Watson, glad of the air and the exercise, set off alone along the path toward Grimpen. The moor lay wide and silent about him, a sea of brown and grey, and the wind from the west was cool upon his face as he left the park behind. For a time he walked freely, enjoying the sense of solitude, and quite forgetting the warnings he had been given.

He had gone about a mile when he heard quick steps behind him, and, turning, he saw a thin, sandy-haired man in a straw hat running toward him with a butterfly net in his hand. The stranger, slightly out of breath, introduced himself as Stapleton of Merripit House and explained that Dr Mortimer had pointed Watson out to him from a distance. His manner was so easy and so friendly that it would have been churlish not to answer in kind.

Slung over his shoulder the naturalist carried a green tin box for his specimens, and he spoke with enthusiasm of the rich butterflies and moths that the moor produced. He added, in the course of conversation, that he had once kept a school in the north of England but that his health had failed, and that he had come to Devonshire for peace and fresh air. Watson listened politely to this pleasant account of a quiet life, and he felt no suspicion whatever.

Presently they came upon a patch of bright green moss, lying between two grey ridges of rock, and Stapleton laid a hand on his companion's arm and warned him to keep well away from it. That, he said, was the Great Grimpen Mire, where a single false step meant death, and only a man who knew every tuft of its edge could cross it alive. He told how he had once seen a pony struggle in it, sinking slowly, until the green mud closed over its head.

As they stood there, a low, sad moan rolled across the moor, deepening and dying away like the voice of some enormous creature in pain. Watson felt the skin creep on the back of his neck, but Stapleton only smiled and said that the sound was made by a bird called the bittern, or perhaps by the mud settling in the Mire. The peasants, he added carelessly, told different stories about it, and he would not repeat them.

Without warning, the naturalist gave a cry of delight, for he had seen a rare butterfly flitting across the bog, and with his net held high he sprang out onto the treacherous green surface. Watson watched in horror as the thin figure leapt from tuft to tuft, never pausing, never slipping, and he fully expected to see him swallowed up by the slime. It was an astonishing display of nerve, and perhaps of something else that he could not name.

While he was still staring after the daring figure, Watson heard a light step, and turning round he saw a woman hurrying toward him through the heather. She was tall, dark-haired and strikingly beautiful, with a pale face, and her eyes were fixed upon his with an expression of the deepest alarm. “Go back,” she cried in a low, urgent voice, “go straight back to London, instantly, and do not ask me why!”

Before he could find any answer, she realised her error, for he was not the man she had taken him for, and she stammered that she had thought him to be Sir Henry Baskerville. At that moment her brother came striding back, flushed and breathless, and remarked, with a sharpness that surprised Watson, that she had been quick to introduce herself. She looked down at the heather without a word, and her face, so full of feeling a moment before, was now a mask.

On the way home Watson passed a hillside covered with the grey circles of ancient huts, where the first men of the moor had made their homes thousands of years before. They stood bare and silent in the setting sun, with here and there a fragment of roof still clinging to the stones, and he reflected idly that a man might hide among them for weeks without being found. The thought, though he did not know it, was to prove more useful than he imagined.

At the Hall, over dinner by the great fireplace, he described the adventure to Sir Henry, who heard him with amused interest and asked a good many questions about the lady. When the young man had gone to bed, Watson drew paper and pen toward him and began the first of the long letters that he had promised to send to Holmes. He wrote slowly, for there was a great deal to tell, and little of it fitted together.

That night, by the light of a single candle, Watson wrote his first long report to Holmes, setting down all he had seen since they parted at the station. He described the vast, silent moor, the soldiers who searched it day after day, and the escaped convict whom nobody seemed able to find. He could not leave out the sobbing in the night, though he had no idea what it meant.

In a second part of the letter, he drew up a list of those who lived within reach of the Hall, because Holmes liked to have every name before him. There were the Stapletons at Merripit House, Dr Mortimer in the village of Grimpen, and an elderly gentleman called Mr Frankland, who was famous for his quarrels and was said to be always at law. Watson added that he had formed no opinion of any of them, which was perfectly true.

A week later, as Sir Henry and Watson walked together over the moor, they met Miss Stapleton, who was gentler and more composed than on the day of her strange outburst. She apologised, with a faint blush, for the confusion she had caused, and Sir Henry, who could not take his eyes from her face, listened with an expression that told Watson everything. The young man, it was clear, had been lost since the very first glance, and he did not care who knew it.

Their talk was cut short, however, for Stapleton came striding toward them through the heather with a white face and eyes that blazed with anger. He seized his sister roughly by the arm, ordered her to come away without delay, and she obeyed him without a word, though she turned once to look back. The whole scene lasted scarcely half a minute, and it left the two Englishmen standing like men struck by lightning.

Sir Henry, deeply offended, stared after the couple with his fists on his hips and declared that he had never been treated so rudely in his life. He had done nothing, he said, to deserve such a look from a man he hardly knew, and he meant to ask for an explanation. Watson could offer no answer, for the naturalist's savage behaviour was as great a puzzle to him as to his companion.

Early the next morning, to the surprise of the household, Stapleton himself appeared at the Hall, stood humbly in the great stone hall with his hat in his hands and begged to be forgiven. His sister, he said, was all that he had in the world, and the thought of losing her had made him behave like a madman. Sir Henry, who was never able to bear a grudge, accepted the apology at once and agreed to dine at Merripit House on Friday.

On Friday evening, as the light faded, Sir Henry and Watson set out across the moor and presently came upon a low grey house standing alone among a few stunted trees. It was Merripit House, and to Watson's eyes it seemed the most desolate dwelling that he had ever seen, with the dark moor pressing close on every side. A single lamp burned in the window like a signal to someone far away.

Before dinner their host took them into a little study and proudly showed them his collection, rows of butterflies and moths pinned in glass cases, each with its name carefully written in a small neat hand. He spoke easily of the school which he had kept in the north of England, of the boys he had taught and of the failure of his health that had forced him to retire. It was all very natural, and yet Watson felt a trace of something false in it.

At the dinner table Miss Stapleton scarcely uttered a word and ate hardly anything, keeping her eyes fixed upon her plate except when she thought no one was looking. Twice Watson caught her glancing at Sir Henry with an expression of undisguised fear, while her brother laughed, filled their glasses and talked of the moor with every sign of cheerfulness. He wondered how a man could be so genial and a woman so afraid in the same room.

They walked home across the dark moor under a sky crowded with stars, and for a long time neither of them spoke, for each was occupied with his own thoughts of the evening. Then, from somewhere in the darkness beyond the rocks, there rose a long, deep, mournful howl that seemed to come from the very earth, and both men stopped dead. Watson's hand went at once to the revolver in his pocket, and the cry rolled slowly away into the silence.

One night, soon after the dinner at Merripit, Watson woke suddenly to the sound of a soft footstep in the corridor, and through the crack of his door he saw a thin yellow light moving along the passage. He rose, opened the door a little way and caught sight of Barrymore creeping past in his stockings, a lighted candle in his hand, with the stealth of a man who did not wish to be seen. It was not the walk of an honest servant going about his duties, and Watson's suspicions awoke at once.

Watson followed him at a distance, keeping to the shadows, until the butler reached the end of the passage, where an uncurtained window looked out across the dark moor. There Barrymore stood motionless, holding the candle against the glass, and he remained so for a long time, as though he were sending a message to someone far away. At last he lowered the light and glided back to his room, and Watson crept after him in silence.

At breakfast he told Sir Henry what he had seen, and the young baronet, who had little patience for secrets in his own house, wished to ask the butler at once. Watson, however, persuaded him to wait, for it seemed wiser to catch the man in the act than to give him a chance to prepare an excuse. They agreed that they would sit up the following night and watch the passage together.

Accordingly, when the next night came, the two men settled themselves in Sir Henry's room with the door ajar and waited in the darkness, hour after hour, while the great clock below counted out the quarters. It struck one, then two, and Watson, who had begun to nod, was just considering whether they had been mistaken when a stealthy step sounded in the corridor. Without a word the two men rose, slipped on their coats and followed the sound stealthily along the dark corridor.

In their stockinged feet they glided after the creeping light and found Barrymore in an empty room at the end of the house, with the candle pressed against the window. Sir Henry flung open the door and demanded, in a voice of thunder, what he was doing, and the unhappy butler started so violently that he almost let the light fall. For a moment he was too frightened to speak at all, and he simply stared at them with his mouth open.

Barrymore stood there, white to the lips and shaking from head to foot, and he swore that it was nothing, only a private affair of his own which he could not explain. When Sir Henry pressed him sternly, he broke down and confessed that the candle was a signal, and that someone out upon the moor was waiting for it each night. It was clear that he had hoped never to be asked, and that the secret had weighed upon him for many weeks.

At that moment Mrs Barrymore appeared in the doorway, her face wet with tears, and the whole sad story came pouring out between them. The man on the moor was Selden, the escaped convict, who was her own younger brother, and she had cared for him since he was a child and could not bear to see him hunted like an animal. It was his sufferings, not any crime of her own, that had made her cry in the night.

While they stood there in the silent room, Watson glanced out of the window and saw, far off in the blackness, a tiny yellow spark that glowed and was gone and glowed again. Sir Henry, who had been listening in grim silence, declared that it was the convict's reply and that he meant to go out at once and take the man himself. Barrymore, wringing his hands, begged them not to, but the young baronet would not be moved.

Armed with their revolvers, and with Barrymore pointing out the direction as well as he could, the two Englishmen hurried out across the moor under a bright and cloudless moon. They had not gone far when they saw a wild, bearded figure bounding from rock to rock ahead, and they pursued him with all speed, stumbling over stones in the dark. The creature ran like a deer, and every time they gained a little ground it vanished among the boulders.

Selden, who knew every hollow of the ground, outran them easily and vanished into the night, leaving the two men breathless and defeated beside a pile of boulders. As Watson turned back, however, he saw a sight that drove the convict from his mind, for on the crest of a high rock stood a tall, thin man, black against the moon. He stood perfectly still, as though watching the two Englishmen from a great distance, and then in an instant he was gone.

The next morning Barrymore thanked the two Englishmen with a humility that was almost painful, and he assured them that the convict would soon leave the country for South America. Sir Henry, whose anger had faded during the night, went upstairs and returned with a bundle of his own old clothes, which he handed to the butler for Selden's use. It was a generous act, though neither of them could guess what strange consequences it would one day have.

Before leaving, Barrymore lowered his voice and told Watson something that sent the recollection of the tall figure on the rock racing through his mind. Selden, it appeared, had seen another man hiding on the moor, a man whom he did not know and did not trust, and he feared that the stranger was a spy. Watson thanked the butler quietly and said nothing of what he had seen himself.

Barrymore then confided that, after Sir Charles's death, he had found a scrap of burned paper among the ashes in the study fireplace, and he had kept it ever since. Only a few words survived the flames, begging the reader to burn the letter and to be at the gate by ten o'clock, and at the bottom were two letters, L L. It was the first real clue that Watson had been given, and he handled it as carefully as if it were a jewel.

Dr Mortimer, to whom the scrap was shown that afternoon, thought for a moment and then declared that the initials could only mean Laura Lyons, a young woman of Coombe Tracey. She was the daughter of the quarrelsome Mr Frankland, who had refused to speak to her since she had married an artist who afterward deserted her. The doctor added, with some embarrassment, that Sir Charles had been among those who had helped her in her distress.

Resolved to visit her at once, Watson set out for Coombe Tracey, and on the way he passed the gate of Lafter Hall, where a red-faced, white-haired old man was waving his stick at an imaginary trespasser. It was Mr Frankland, who greeted him with the delight of a man starved of an audience, and began to describe his numerous lawsuits as though they were glorious military campaigns. Watson, to his own surprise, found him oddly likeable, for there was something touching in the old man's simple vanity.

Not content with talk, the old gentleman led Watson up onto his flat roof, where a large brass telescope stood pointed toward the distant hills of the moor. He explained that he spent his days watching for the escaped convict, and Watson, looking through the glass, was startled to see how clearly it showed the road and the gates of the Hall. It was an instrument, he reflected, that could see a great deal, and perhaps more than its owner understood.

At Coombe Tracey a maid showed Watson into a small, neat sitting room, where a young woman sat at a table beside a typewriter. Laura Lyons was slim and graceful, with large dark eyes and soft red hair, and though she was plainly alarmed by the visit of a stranger, she received him with a pleasant dignity. Her fingers, however, would not be still, and they played nervously with the edge of the table.

When Watson told her that he knew of the burned letter, she twisted her handkerchief into a knot and, after a moment's hesitation, admitted that it was hers. She had been in terrible difficulties, she said, and needed money to obtain her freedom from a husband who had abandoned her, and in her desperation she had written to Sir Charles to beg his help. It was an honest confession, and it made her seem more human and less guilty.

She went on to say that she had asked Sir Charles to meet her at the gate on the night of his death, but she insisted that she had never gone there at all. The request that he should burn the letter, she explained, had been written only because she could not bear to have her private misery discovered by anyone in the neighbourhood. Watson listened carefully, for there was a note in her voice that did not ring entirely true.

When he asked why she had stayed away, she said that a friend had advised her against it, and when he asked the friend's name she lifted her chin and refused to speak. Watson, who could not force a confession from a lady, took his leave with a bow, but he was convinced that she was shielding someone whose name was of the greatest importance. As he walked away down the quiet lane, he wondered who could have such power over her.

On his way home Watson was hailed once more by Mr Frankland, who was beckoning wildly from the roof of Lafter Hall, and who pointed his telescope toward a distant rocky hill. For several days, the old man declared, he had watched a boy carrying a bundle of food along the same path to the same tor, and he was certain that the supplies were meant for the escaped convict. Watson looked through the glass and saw a tiny figure toiling up the slope.

At the Hall, Sir Henry announced that he was to dine at Merripit House that evening, and Watson, who did not like the idea, decided to settle the question of the hut at once. If he hurried, he calculated, he could climb the tor in the afternoon and be back in time to walk across the moor with his friend. It was a small risk, he thought, and the daylight was still good, so he took his stick and set out at once.

The path to the tor was steep and stony, and the afternoon sun beat down upon it without a breath of wind to cool the air. Watson climbed slowly, one hand upon his revolver, pausing now and then to look about him, and from the summit he gazed down upon a wide sweep of empty moor, in which nothing moved but a single hawk. It seemed hard to believe that any living man was hidden in such a place.

On the top of the hill stood a ring of ancient stone huts, and one of them still kept half of its roof, so that it offered a snug retreat for anyone who wished to be unseen. Inside he found a rolled blanket, several tins of preserved food, an empty water bottle and a few ends of cigarettes, and he realised that somebody had been living there in comfort for a good while. The place had the neat, orderly air of a soldier's camp, and it was plainly the work of a practised hand.

On a flat stone beside the blanket lay a half sheet of paper, and Watson, picking it up, felt a cold shudder run down his back as he read it. It was written in a small, clear hand, and it stated simply that Dr Watson had gone to Coombe Tracey, which was precisely what he had done that very morning. Someone, then, had been following his every movement, and had been reporting it to someone else.

He stood very still, straining his ears, and presently he heard from outside the sharp click of a boot upon the stones, coming nearer with a slow, deliberate tread. Drawing his revolver, Watson slipped into a dark corner of the hut and held his breath, and a moment later a long shadow fell across the threshold. It was an unnerving moment, and his finger tightened on the trigger while he waited to see who would enter.

“It's a lovely evening, my dear Watson,” said a familiar and perfectly calm voice, “and I really think that you will be more comfortable outside than in.” Watson stared, scarcely able to believe his own eyes, for in the doorway, with the last of the sunlight behind him and his thin face lit by a smile, stood Sherlock Holmes. He was a little browner and a good deal dirtier than in London, but his eyes were as bright as ever.

Holmes explained, with an apology that was not entirely sincere, that he had never been in London at all, but had come down in secret to study the moor with his own eyes. Had he arrived openly, he said, the enemy would have been warned and would have altered his plans, and so for several days he had lived in this old hut like a man of the Stone Age. He added, with a straight face, that he had been very comfortable indeed, and that the cooking had not troubled him.

The lonely figure that Watson had seen on the rock against the moon, he went on, had been himself, and the boy who carried food to the tor was Cartwright, who brought him bread and linen. Holmes also admitted that he had read every one of Watson's reports with the greatest care, and that they had proved far more valuable than his friend could suspect. Watson, half hurt and half pleased, did not know whether to scold him or to laugh.

Watson then described his interview with Laura Lyons, and Holmes listened with his eyes half closed, nodding slowly at each point as though a great puzzle were falling into place. Suddenly he sat up and asked sharply where Sir Henry was, and when Watson answered that he was dining that evening at Merripit House, the detective sprang to his feet and snatched up his hat. His face had changed, and Watson understood at once that something dreadful was near.

Holmes and Watson hurried down the hillside as the sun sank behind the moor and the long shadows of the rocks reached out across the heather. Holmes spoke hardly a word, but his thin face was set in a hard and anxious line, and Watson, who had seen him in many dangers, had never seen him so troubled. The pleasant hours in the hut seemed suddenly to belong to another world, and the peace of the afternoon was gone.

They struck a narrow path that led toward Merripit House, and the sky darkened rapidly above them while the first stars pricked out one by one in the east. Holmes told Watson, in a low and urgent voice, that he feared for Sir Henry's walk home that night, and he took out his revolver and examined it as they went. It was a warning that no explanation could have made clearer, and Watson felt his own pulse quicken.

They were still some distance from the house when a terrible scream tore the silence of the evening to pieces, a loud, high, horrible cry that seemed to come from a man in the very depth of mortal terror. Holmes stopped as if he had been shot, and Watson felt his friend's fingers close upon his arm like iron. It was a sound that neither of them would ever forget, a cry that seemed to hang in the darkness long after it had died.

They ran toward the cry as fast as the uneven ground allowed, tripping over stones and tearing through bushes, but the sound had already died into nothing, and the moor lay silent again under the darkening sky. Then, from a long way off, there came a deep, mournful howl that rose and fell and slowly faded, and Watson felt his heart turn cold within him. Holmes cursed under his breath, drew his revolver and ran faster over the stones, with Watson stumbling at his heels.

They came at last to a cluster of broken rocks and, at the foot of a steep slope, they saw a dark shape lying on the ground. It was a man, stretched face downward, with his head bent under him at an angle that no living neck could bear, and he lay as motionless as the stones about him. Watson drew in his breath sharply, for even in the darkness the figure seemed horribly familiar to him.

Holmes struck a match, shielded it with his hand and held it above the body, and its small, trembling flame showed a pale face and a thick, black, unkempt beard. Watson recognised it at once, and with a cry of horror he exclaimed that the dead man was Selden, the convict who had escaped from Princetown. The wild eyes were wide open, and even in death they held a look of terror.

The dead man wore a tweed suit which Watson knew only too well, because it was the one that Sir Henry had given to Barrymore for his wife's unhappy brother. In a moment Holmes understood what this meant, and he explained, in a voice that shook with relief and anger, that the hound had followed the scent of Sir Henry's clothes. The wrong man had died in the right man's place, mistaken by the beast for the heir whom it had been trained to hunt.

They searched the slope and the rocks all around the body, Holmes even kneeling to listen for the heavy tread of a great animal, but they found no trace of any beast, and nothing moved among the shadows. The only sound was the faint echo of the distant howl, which grew weaker with every moment and at last disappeared into the silence. It was as though the hound had melted into the night, leaving behind it only a dead man and a deeper silence.

They were still standing beside the body when they heard a quick step on the path, and a thin figure came hurrying out of the darkness with a butterfly net slung over his shoulder. It was Stapleton, who greeted Watson with astonishment and then asked, in a voice that trembled slightly, whether it was Sir Henry who had been hurt. He seemed to be gasping for breath, as though he had been running for a long time.

Then, as the light of a second match fell upon the face of Holmes, Stapleton stopped short, and Watson saw a swift change pass over his features, like a mask being drawn tight. Holmes introduced himself with perfect calm, and the naturalist replied with polite words of welcome, but when his eyes dropped to the dead man, the expression on his face was something more like disappointment than grief. It was gone in an instant, but Watson had seen it, and he stored the memory carefully away.

Stapleton asked, in a voice of perfect concern, how the convict had come to his end, and Holmes replied that the man had fallen from the rocks while running in the dark. The naturalist murmured that it was a sad business, but that at least the countryside was now freed from a danger, and he promised to send a message to the police at the earliest hour. Then he bowed politely to the two detectives and went off alone into the night, swinging his net.

As soon as he was out of hearing, Holmes took Watson by the arm and whispered that the naturalist's first question had been about Sir Henry, and that he had shown no sorrow for the convict. It was a small thing, he added, and one that no jury would have taken seriously, but he had spent his whole life collecting small things. Watson, glancing at his friend's grave face in the starlight, did not argue, for he had learned to respect such hints.

At dawn the two men walked to the Hall, where Sir Henry sat at breakfast with a pale face, and he sprang up with a cry of joy when he saw the great detective in the doorway. He had been told nothing of the hut or of the long deception, and he wrung Holmes's hand as though he would never let it go. Holmes, a little embarrassed, begged him to forgive the secrecy and to sit down.

With great gentleness Holmes told Barrymore that Selden was dead, and the butler bowed his head and stood silent for a long time, his big hands hanging helplessly at his sides. In the kitchen, Mrs Barrymore began to weep quietly, and Sir Henry, deeply moved, promised that the poor man should have a decent burial and that no blame would be laid upon those who had helped him. It was the one act of simple kindness in a day of horrors, and everyone in the kitchen felt its warmth.

That afternoon Holmes asked to be shown the portrait gallery, and he walked slowly down the long, dim room with a lamp in his hand. He paused before each picture as though he were reading a book, until at last he stood for a long time in front of Hugo Baskerville. It was a handsome cavalier in a wide hat, with long curls and a lace collar, who gazed down on him with an air of cold amusement.

He lifted a hand and covered the cavalier's hat and the long curls that framed the face, and then he stepped back and invited Watson to look. For a moment Watson saw only an old picture of a stranger who had been dead for centuries. Then, with a shock that made him catch his breath, he saw the thin, sharp features of Stapleton staring out of the canvas, with the same eyes, the same chin and the same hard mouth.

Holmes explained, in a low and steady voice, that the face had come down through the family as the family's blood had done, and that Stapleton must be a Baskerville of the old line. It was the key to everything, he said, for it showed that the naturalist had a reason, which no one had suspected, for wishing to see Sir Henry out of the way. A mystery that had seemed to be one of ghosts was becoming a matter of heirs.

The next morning Holmes and Watson drove over to Coombe Tracey and called on Laura Lyons, who received them in her small sitting room with a face of great alarm. Holmes told her politely but firmly that he knew she had not told Dr Watson the whole truth, and that he had come to lay before her what he already knew. She tried to answer, but the words would not come, and she sank slowly into the chair beside the window.

Holmes said that the friend whose name she had refused to give was Stapleton, and that the lady who lived with him at Merripit House was not his sister, as everyone supposed, but his lawful wife. Laura Lyons stared at him for a long moment as though she had not understood a word. Then she covered her face with her hands, for Stapleton had promised to marry her as soon as her divorce was complete.

At last, weeping and angry, she told them that Stapleton had dictated her letter to Sir Charles and had then forbidden her to keep the appointment. Holmes wrote down every word of it with the quiet patience of a man who has waited long for a statement. That evening, when the train drew up at the little country station, a small, sallow, sharp-eyed man in a brown suit stepped down from it, and Holmes greeted Inspector Lestrade of Scotland Yard with a smile of relief.

That evening, in the library of the Hall, Holmes drew a rough map upon a sheet of paper and laid out his plan before Sir Henry and the newly arrived Lestrade. The hound, he said, could only be taken if its master believed he still had a chance to strike, and no better lure existed than the man it had been trained to hunt. It was a cruel proposal, and Holmes did not pretend otherwise, but he saw no other way to catch so careful a murderer.

Sir Henry listened with a steady face and, to Watson's admiration, accepted the proposal without a moment's hesitation, though his hands were not entirely still upon the arms of his chair. He would go to Merripit House for dinner, as he had been invited, and he would walk home across the moor alone, like a man who suspected nothing. Watson thought that he had never seen courage of a quieter and finer kind.

Holmes took care to let it be known at Merripit that he and Watson had been called back to London on urgent business, so that the naturalist should believe the coast was clear. To Sir Henry he gave the strictest orders, that he must keep to the path, that he must on no account run toward the Mire, and that whatever he might hear he must trust that his friends were near. These instructions he repeated twice over, and he made the young man say them back to him word for word.

At dusk on the evening of the dinner, Holmes, Watson and Lestrade walked out onto the moor, each with a loaded revolver in his coat. Lestrade, a small, sallow, tough man who had chased criminals through every back street of London, grumbled at the darkness and the damp, but he followed where Holmes led. He had been told about the hound and had received the news with the cold politeness of one who did not believe a word of it.

Holmes brought them to a group of tall boulders, about two hundred yards from the front door of Merripit House, where they could see the lamplit windows and the whole length of the path Sir Henry must follow home. There they crouched behind the stones, and as the last of the daylight faded, the cold crept into their bones and the silence of the moor settled around them. Nobody dared even to cough, and the only sound was the faint rustle of the wind in the dry heather.

While they waited, Holmes looked out across the moor and saw a long, low line of white vapour rising slowly from the direction of the Grimpen Mire, and his face grew grave. He muttered that the fog was an enemy they had not counted upon, for it might hide the path altogether and spoil every arrangement. Even Lestrade, peering over the rock at the creeping whiteness, forgot for once to grumble about the cold.

The mist grew thicker with every minute and crept steadily closer, until it swirled about the rocks in cold, clinging clouds that wet the faces of the three men. Holmes lay down with his ear to the ground, listened for a moment, and then led the others quietly forward until they were crouching close beside the path. It was a risk, but a necessary one, for a man who passes unseen in such a fog may die unseen.

The windows of Merripit House shone pale and yellow through the fog, like the eyes of some sleeping animal, and the hours seemed to crawl past on leaden feet. No one spoke, and Watson found himself counting the beats of his own heart, while the cold mist settled on his coat in tiny drops. From time to time he thought that he heard a distant sound, and each time he was not sure.

At last the door of the house swung open, and a stream of lamplight poured out across the grass, and in the middle of it stood Sir Henry, who said a cheerful good night to his hosts. Then the door closed, the light vanished, and the young man set off along the path with a firm step, whistling softly to himself, as if there were nothing in the world to fear. Watson's throat was dry, and he could hear nothing but the pounding of his own heart and the soft fall of the young man's boots.

Holmes took Lestrade by the wrist and whispered to them both to be ready, as the fog rolled in over the whole path like a great white wall. Sir Henry's footsteps came nearer, and then, out of the whiteness behind him, Watson heard a soft, steady, pattering sound, like the paws of some heavy animal. His fingers closed tightly round his revolver, and he strained his eyes into the whiteness, waiting for a shape to appear.

Sir Henry passed within a few yards of the hiding place, whistling softly and looking straight ahead along the path, with no idea that three pairs of eyes were fixed upon him from the rocks. Holmes held his breath and, with a gesture of his hand, warned his companions not to stir until the moment came. It was the longest minute that Watson had ever known, and he felt the sweat run cold upon his forehead.

Then, out of the white fog behind the young man, there sprang a huge, coal-black hound as large as a small lion, with a mouth and a pair of eyes that glowed with a hellish fire. It was no ghost, and yet its fierce silence and its burning face made it seem like a nightmare risen from the earth. Lestrade, with a cry of horror, flung himself flat upon the ground, and Watson heard him groan among the stones.

The beast bounded past the boulders where they crouched, and Holmes, Watson and the groaning Lestrade fired together into the mist, and Watson heard a howl that told him one of the bullets had gone home. But the hound did not stop, nor even slacken its pace, and it flew on along the path after the young man with long, savage bounds. The shots seemed to have no more effect on it than hail upon a roof, and the glowing shape never swerved.

Sir Henry, hearing the noise, glanced over his shoulder and saw the great glowing shape rushing at him through the fog, and with a scream of terror he began to run. But no man could have outrun that creature, and with one tremendous spring it leapt upon his back and hurled him to the ground, its burning jaws reaching for his throat. It was the moment toward which the whole case had been moving, and every man there knew that it would decide everything.

Holmes was after it in a moment, running like a man possessed, and he pressed his revolver against the creature's side and fired five shots, one after another, into its body. With a last great howl of rage and pain, the hound rolled over upon the grass, kicked wildly for a moment with its great paws and then lay still. Silence fell upon the moor, broken only by the heavy breathing of the men.

Sir Henry lay stretched upon the grass in a faint, and Holmes, bending over him, found with a rush of relief that he was alive and quite unhurt, though his face was as white as paper. Beside him sprawled the huge body of the hound, entirely dead, and about its muzzle and throat there clung a faint blue light, like the glimmer of a dying candle. It was a strange and ghastly sight, and Watson could scarcely believe that so wild a creature had been made by the hand of man.

Holmes reached out and touched the glowing jaws, and when he held up his hand, Watson saw that his fingers were shining in the darkness, as though they had been dipped in fire. It was a chemical called phosphorus, he said, and some wicked brain had smeared it upon the animal's coat to turn a living dog into a creature of horror. Whoever had done it had known well how to turn a man's fear against himself.

Watson ran to the young baronet and poured a little brandy from a flask between his lips, and presently Sir Henry opened his eyes and stared round in bewilderment. Holmes told him gently that the monster which had followed his family for two hundred years was nothing worse than a large dog, and that it was dead. The young man laughed unsteadily, and the colour began to return to his face.

Lestrade, who had recovered from his astonishment and was now ashamed of having fallen upon his face, remained beside the body of the hound, while Holmes and Watson hurried to Merripit House. The front door stood wide open, and they searched the dark rooms one after another with their revolvers in their hands, but there was no sign of the master of the house. The place was as silent as a tomb, and their footsteps echoed on the bare boards as they went from room to room.

At last, from an upper floor, they heard a faint, dull thumping, and in a bedroom they found a woman fastened to a post with strips of sheet, a cloth tied over her mouth. It was Beryl Stapleton, pale and exhausted, and Holmes cut her bonds with his knife while Watson found her a glass of water. She looked at them with eyes full of terror and relief, and for a moment she could not speak.

When Beryl had recovered a little and had drunk some water, Holmes asked her gently who she was, and she told him in a low and weary voice that she was Stapleton's lawful wife. For years her husband had forced her to pass as his sister, because he said that it would serve his plans, and she had obeyed him out of fear. Tonight, when she had dared at last to refuse him, he had bound her with his own hands and left her in the dark.

She told them that her husband had fled into the Mire when he learned that the hound was dead, and that a secret path, marked with white sticks, led through the bog to a lonely island. Nobody else, she said, knew the way, and a stranger who tried to follow it in the dark would be lost before he had taken twenty steps. Her voice shook when she spoke of it, for she knew that her husband had gone where no one could follow him.

Holmes and Watson carried the still-trembling Sir Henry to Merripit House and laid him on a sofa by the fire, while the fog pressed against the windows like a grey blanket. It was impossible to follow any man across the Mire in such darkness, and Holmes, with great reluctance, agreed that they must wait for the morning. It was a night of anxious watching for everybody in the house, and none of them closed an eye until dawn.

At dawn the fog began to thin and roll back, and the sun rose upon a wide and silent bog, bright green in the pale light and as peaceful as a meadow. Beryl, who had not slept, led them to the place where the hidden path began, and Holmes thanked her with an earnestness that surprised her, for she had expected only reproaches. Then they set out in single file toward the heart of the Mire, with Beryl pointing out the first of the white sticks.

Holmes, Watson and Lestrade followed the white sticks one by one, stepping with great care on the firm tufts and keeping clear of the black pools that gleamed on either side. The ground trembled beneath them and sucked at their boots with a faint, sullen noise, and Watson, as he walked, did not allow himself to think what would happen if he slipped. A single mistake would have ended the matter, and none of the three men would ever have been seen again.

On a small island in the middle of the bog, they found the ruins of an ancient mine, and in a cavity under its broken roof stood a thick iron stake with a heavy chain still fastened to it. Around the stake lay a litter of gnawed bones, and the whole place had the sour, animal smell of a kennel, so that there could be no doubt that they had found the lair of the hound. Lestrade, who had been silent for an hour, swore softly under his breath and admitted that he had never seen such a place.

On their way back along the path, Holmes suddenly stopped and stooped, and from the sucking mud at the side of the track he lifted an old black boot, caked with slime. He turned it over in his hands with the quiet satisfaction of a man who has found a missing page, and told Watson that it was the very boot that had been stolen from Sir Henry's hotel in London. It had come a long way to lie in this lonely place, and it told its story more plainly than any witness.

The explanation, said Holmes, was simple, for the thief had first taken a new boot, which bears no scent and is useless to a hound, and had then returned it and taken an old one. Stapleton had held the old boot to the dog's nose, and the creature had learned the smell of Sir Henry as a man learns a face. It was, Holmes said, a masterpiece of cold and patient cruelty, and he spoke of it with something like disgust.

They followed the path to the place where the white sticks ended, and there they found a line of footprints that led straight to a wide pool of green slime, as smooth as glass. It was plain that Stapleton, blinded by the fog and the fear of capture, had missed the way and stepped into the deep mud, and that he had never come out again. Not a bubble stirred on the surface, and the whole green stillness seemed to mock the men who stood watching it.

For many hours they searched the edges of the bog with poles and ropes, but they found no sign of the naturalist, living or dead. At last Holmes stood looking out over the still green water, and he said very quietly that the Mire never gives up what it takes, and that perhaps it was better so. Nobody answered him, and the only sound was the cry of a bird over the empty moor.

Some days later, when Sir Henry was strong enough to sit up for an evening, the four men gathered round the great fire in the hall, and Holmes filled his pipe and lit it with a spill. He said that he would explain the whole case in its proper order, beginning at the beginning, and he warned them that the story was not a pleasant one. Watson, who knew his friend's habits, settled back in his chair to listen, and the others did the same.

The man whom they had known as Stapleton, Holmes said, had in truth been a Baskerville, the son of Rodger Baskerville, who was the younger brother of Sir Charles. It was the old family blood that he had seen in the portrait in the gallery, and it explained, as nothing else could, why this stranger had such an interest in the estate. The likeness, he added, had been the thread that drew all the others together.

Rodger, according to Holmes, had been the black sheep of the family, a young man who had disgraced the name and had been obliged to leave England for Central America, where he was reported to have died of fever. Everyone had believed that he had died unmarried and without children, and no one in Devonshire had thought to question the report. They had all been mistaken, as Holmes was about to show, and the truth was far stranger than the report.

In truth, Rodger had married abroad and had left a son, who grew up to become a schoolmaster in the north of England under a different name, and who had a school of his own in Yorkshire. When one of his pupils died of a fever, however, the school lost its reputation and failed, and the schoolmaster, deeply in debt, left the district in a hurry and began a new life elsewhere. It was a clever way of burying the past, though it could not bury the family face.

He took the name of Stapleton and moved south with his wife Beryl, a beautiful girl of Costa Rica whom he had married abroad, and who had believed that she was marrying a gentleman. His love of butterflies and moths, which was perfectly genuine, gave him an excuse to settle in the quiet moorland of Devonshire, where nobody would think to ask who he was. It was the perfect cover for a long and patient game, and he played it without a single slip for years.

In Devonshire, Holmes continued, he soon learned that only two lives stood between him and the fortune: the old and childless Sir Charles, whose heart was weak, and the young heir in Canada. If both could be removed, the estate would be his, and nobody on earth would suspect the shy naturalist of Merripit House. It was a plan of terrible simplicity, and it needed nothing but patience, a dog and a good deal of cunning.

Holmes turned with great kindness to Dr Mortimer, who had gone pale, and assured him that he was not to blame for having told his neighbour of Sir Charles's weak heart and of the old legend of the hound. No honest man could have guessed what use would be made of such talk, he said, and the real fault lay with the clever and wicked mind that had listened so attentively. The doctor bowed his head, a little comforted, though the shadow of his old friend's death still lay upon his face.

Stapleton had resolved, Holmes said, to make the legend his weapon, and with this in view he had bought in London a huge dog, part mastiff and part bloodhound, and brought it down by train in great secrecy. He hid it in the old tin mine on the island in the Grimpen Mire, where nobody but himself dared to venture, and fed it there like a prisoner. It was a lair that no policeman would have thought to search, and no honest man would have dared to enter.

To complete the illusion, the villain had smeared the animal's coat and muzzle with a paste made of phosphorus, which gleamed with a ghostly light in the darkness and made a flesh-and-blood dog seem like a creature from the pit. He had trained it with infinite patience to hunt on command, and it would run down whatever scent he gave it. Watson shivered as he thought of the gentle man who had shown him his butterflies.

There remained the difficulty of bringing Sir Charles to the moor gate in the dark, and for this Stapleton made use of Laura Lyons, whom he had won by a promise of marriage and who was desperate for money. He told her what to write to Sir Charles, begged for an appointment at the gate at ten o'clock, and Sir Charles, who was always generous to a lady in trouble, went there on the fatal evening. He did not know that a more terrible visitor was also expected, and that it would arrive on four silent feet.

Holmes went on to describe the fatal night at the gate, where Sir Charles had waited for a lady who did not come, since Stapleton had forbidden Laura Lyons to leave her house. Instead, out of the darkness at the far end of the alley, there came bounding toward him the great glowing hound, its jaws and eyes shining like a creature from the pit. The old man had never in his life seen anything so terrible, and for a moment he stood frozen to the spot.

Sir Charles, who had a weak heart and a great fear of the family curse, turned and ran for his life down the long dark avenue of yew trees. Dr Mortimer, listening, suddenly recalled that the marks upon the gravel had shown a man running upon his toes, and somewhere along that path the old man's heart had given way. He fell dead of terror before the hound had so much as touched him, and the animal had killed him without a bite.

Stapleton, said Holmes, had then called off his dog and gone quietly home across the moor, perfectly confident that no one could ever prove a crime against him. What English court, after all, would believe that a gentleman had murdered his uncle by means of a phosphorescent dog, and what jury could be asked to convict upon the evidence of a legend? His security, in fact, had been almost complete, and he went to bed that night as peacefully as any honest man.

When the new heir came from Canada, Stapleton and his wife had followed him up to London, where they stayed in a modest hotel and watched his every movement. The naturalist disguised himself in a thick black beard, which explained the mysterious cab and the stranger who had borrowed Holmes's own name with such impudence. Barrymore, whom Holmes's telegram had placed at the Hall that very day, had never been the bearded man at all, and Watson could not help laughing at the memory of the cabman's grin.

The warning letter, Holmes revealed, had been sent in secret by Beryl herself, who had cut the words from the newspaper out of fear for Sir Henry and had prayed that the warning would turn him back. In the very first moment of the case, he had noticed a faint scent of white jessamine upon the paper, and that small perfume had told him that a woman was involved. The mystery had been in his hands from the very start, though he had not yet known how to read it.

As for the boots, he went on, a hotel servant had been bribed to take them, and a new boot, having no smell of the wearer, was useless to the hound, so an old one was stolen instead. This old boot Stapleton had held under the animal's nose before every hunt, and Holmes had found it himself in the mud of the Mire. It was the last link in a long chain, and Holmes spoke of it with a quiet and professional pride.

Stapleton had intended to use his wife's beauty to draw Sir Henry to Merripit, but she had refused to take part in any plan that would harm the young man, and her husband, in his fury, had threatened her. When Sir Henry began genuinely to admire her, the naturalist's temper, which had been held in check for years, finally broke loose, and it was jealousy and not strategy that drove him out onto the moor that day. A plain human passion had nearly spoiled a perfect crime, as it so often does, and Holmes smiled at the irony.

On the night of the scream, Holmes said, the kind gift of old clothes that Sir Henry had made to the butler had been the cause of the convict's death, since the hound had followed their scent. The poor wretch had run blindly through the darkness, had fallen from a rock and broken his neck, and the creature that pursued him had run on, finding that it had been tracking the wrong man. It was a grim irony, and it showed how a single act of kindness may turn into a snare.

Holmes frowned and admitted that he had taken a great risk in using Sir Henry as bait, and that if the fog had come a few minutes earlier, the plan might have ended in disaster. Yet he insisted that he could not have won his case in any other way, for no jury would have believed the story of a ghostly dog unless a real one had been laid before them. Sir Henry only smiled and shook his head, saying that he had trusted Holmes from the first and did not regret it.

At last Holmes finished his long narrative and leaned back in his chair, and for some time no one in the great hall said a word, for each man was thinking of the dead and the living. The only sound was the slow, steady ticking of the old clock in the corner, and presently, to the surprise of them all, it began to strike twelve. The sound rolled softly through the empty rooms of the house, as though the old Hall itself were sighing with relief.

In the days that followed, Sir Henry woke at night more than once, trembling at the memory of the terrible creature that had sprung upon him out of the fog, and Dr Mortimer examined him with a grave face. The doctor declared that nothing could mend such shaken nerves except a long rest and a sea voyage, and the young baronet, after a moment's hesitation, agreed to travel round the world with him. It seemed the wisest of all remedies, and Sir Henry, who loved adventure, began almost to look forward to it.

On a grey morning, Selden was buried in the quiet churchyard at Grimpen, and only a handful of people stood by the grave. Barrymore held his hat in both hands and stared at the ground, while his wife, who had wept so many nights in secret, stood beside him at last composed and silent. It was a simple ceremony, but Sir Henry had seen to it that the poor man had everything that decency required.

A little later Barrymore came to Sir Henry, twisting his cap in his hands, and said respectfully that he and his wife wished to leave the Hall and its service. Sir Charles had left them a small legacy, he explained, and they intended to start a modest business of their own in some place far from the moor, where nobody would look at them with pity. Sir Henry, who understood, shook his hand warmly and promised every help that it was in his power to give.

One afternoon Mr Frankland arrived at the Hall, as red-faced and cheerful as ever, and announced to the company that his famous telescope had played the chief part in the solution of the whole mystery. Holmes listened with a gravity that Watson could only admire, and then thanked the old gentleman most sincerely for his assistance, a courtesy that sent Frankland away in the best of humours. It cost the detective nothing, and it made one lonely and quarrelsome old man very happy for the rest of the day.

Lestrade, who liked his criminals tidy, thought that Laura Lyons ought to be charged with something, but Holmes shook his head and argued the matter quietly with him on the platform of the little station. She had been deceived, he said, by a clever and unscrupulous man who had promised her marriage, and she had never known that the letter would bring Sir Charles to his death. In the end the inspector gave way, though not without a long grumble about the untidiness of the law.

Beryl gave her full statement to the police and was permitted to go, and she left the moor early one morning, carrying a single small bag and wrapped in a grey shawl. She wished only to live quietly somewhere far from Dartmoor, and she thanked Holmes in a low voice for having believed that she had been more victim than accomplice. Watson watched her go with a feeling of pity, and no little respect for the courage that she had shown at the end.

Sir Henry, who was growing stronger by the day, walked slowly through the great hall and, one by one, threw open the tall windows so that the sunlight came pouring in upon the dark panels and the faded portraits. He said that he meant to fill the old house with light and with friends, as his uncle had always intended, and that the gloom of the Baskervilles should end with him. It was the first time Watson had heard him laugh freely since the night of the hound, and the sound was good to hear.

On their last night at the Hall, Holmes and Watson walked together down the Yew Alley to the little wooden gate that opened upon the moor, and they stood there for a while in silence. The moon was high and bright, the great expanse of heather lay peaceful under it, and for the first time since his arrival Watson looked at the moor and saw nothing more terrible than a lonely and beautiful country. Holmes lit his pipe and said that he thought it would sleep quietly now.

Sir Henry gave a farewell dinner in the long dining room, which for once was bright with candles, and he rose at the end of the meal to thank Holmes and Watson for having saved his life. He said that he would never forget the cold night on the moor, nor the courage of the two friends who had stood between him and a dreadful death, and he drank their health with a trembling hand. Holmes, a little embarrassed, bowed and said that it had been an interesting case.

By the next morning the trunks stood packed in the hall, and the old house was full of the bustle of farewell, with servants carrying bags and Dr Mortimer's spaniel racing in and out between everybody's legs. Sir Henry, pale but smiling, shook hands with each of the household before he went out into the sunshine, and Watson thought that he looked a different man from the one who had arrived. The shadow had lifted from the Hall at last, and even the old portraits on the walls seemed to look kinder.

On the steps of the old house, Sir Henry shook Holmes's hand for a long time and said, with a trace of feeling, that he would return when he had seen the world and grown strong again. He promised that the next time they met, the Hall would be full of light and music and laughter, and that the Baskerville curse would be only a story told to children. Holmes bowed, plainly moved, and said that he looked forward to it more than he could easily say.

The carriage rolled down the long avenue of elms and out along the road that passed Merripit House, which now stood shuttered and silent among its stunted trees, as though ashamed of what it had seen. Holmes did not so much as glance toward it, but Watson noticed a loose curtain flapping in an upstairs window, and he found that he was glad when the bend of the road hid the place from view. The naturalist's butterflies, he supposed, were still pinned in their glass cases, bright and silent and quite forgotten.

As they climbed the hill beyond the village, Watson looked back at the moor, which lay bright and peaceful in the morning light, with purple heather rolling away toward the distant tors. It seemed hardly credible that such a lovely and open country could have held so much terror, and he reflected that the darkness of a place is often only a matter of the hour at which it is seen. The thought was a comfort, and he carried it with him as the carriage rattled down toward the station.

At the little station, Sir Henry and Dr Mortimer took the train for the port where their ship was waiting, and the doctor's spaniel jumped up on the seat between them with a bark of delight. They waved from the carriage window until the train swung round a curve in the line and was lost behind a bank of ferns, and Watson found, to his surprise, that a lump had risen in his throat. He had grown fond of the young baronet during their strange weeks together, and he knew that he would miss him.

Lestrade shook hands with Holmes on the platform and admitted, with the frankness of an honest man, that he would never forget the sight of the glowing hound as long as he lived. Then he touched his hat, picked up his bag and remarked that the Yard would be hearing of this affair for years to come, though he was not sure that they would believe it. Holmes thanked him warmly for his help and for his calm in a very strange hour.

Holmes and Watson settled themselves in an empty carriage, facing each other across a little table, and as the train rattled eastward they talked over the case from beginning to end, picking up each thread in turn. Holmes explained once more a number of small points, the scent of the jessamine, the old boot and the cabman's grin, and Watson, who had missed most of them, marvelled at how many clues he had walked past. His friend only laughed and told him that observation was merely a habit, and that habits can be learned.

Presently Holmes fell silent and gazed out of the window at the flying green fields with a faint, thoughtful smile, and then he remarked that it had been one of the strangest cases of his career. The world was full of clever villains, he said, but few of them had had the audacity to turn a legend, a bog and a dog into a weapon, and fewer still would have come so close to success. He added, with a dry smile, that he would rather have had the dog on his side than on the other.

They reached London after dark, to find a heavy yellow fog hanging over the streets and turning every gas lamp into a blurred and shimmering ball of light. A cab took them slowly through the crowded thoroughfares, with the driver calling to his horse, and Watson felt the noise and bustle of the great city close round him like a welcome after the long silence of the moor. It was good to be home, in the warm and ugly and wonderful city that he had so often wished himself back to.

At the door of Baker Street the faithful Mrs Hudson met them with a cry of delight, and she hurried away to bring tea and a hot supper, scolding Holmes gently for being so thin. Holmes sank down into his old armchair, stretched his long legs toward the bright fire and gave a deep sigh of contentment, while the familiar room, with its cluttered shelves and its smell of tobacco, seemed to wrap them round. Even the clock on the mantelpiece sounded cheerful, and the whole room seemed to say that all was well again.

Later that evening, on a damp and foggy night at Baker Street, Holmes laid his pipe aside, stretched out his legs toward the fire and announced with a smile that he had two tickets for the opera. Watson, who had not seen his friend so relaxed for weeks, laughed aloud and reached for his coat, while the great detective rose, buttoned his own and led the way down the stairs. And as the cab carried them through the lamplit streets, the dark moor and its hound seemed very far away.
